reply_data.body:
In order to "activate" this module, you have to call its `setup()` function with your `config` table (or nothing to use default config). So in your case it should be enough to use this line instead of a posted one:
```lua
setup = [[require('mini.surround').setup()]],  
```

How to make visual selection dot-repeatable with `mini.surround`? For example, with this mapping
```
vim.api.nvim_set_keymap('x', 'S', [[:<C-u>lua MiniSurround.add('visual')<CR>]], { noremap = true })
```
if I select some text in visual mode and then `S"` this will surround selection with double quotes. But I'd like to repeat this action with `.` for the other selection.

reply_data.body:
Unfortunately, not possible at the moment. Couple of reasons:
- In my experience, visual mode operations are not really intended to be dot-repeatable. Operations with text objects and motions - are. I understand that it is possible in the way that you describe, just doesn't seem to be widely implemented and used. 
- If I remember correctly, originally it was somewhat difficult to make properly due to module design.

reply_data.body:
> Is it a real inconvenience to swap f (F) for t (T) manually?
It is not about swapping them in the config, it is about not re-initiating jumps if you overshoot.

For instance, let's say that you did `fo;;;;;;;` and then you realised that you over jumped by three positions and need to go three positions back. 
```lua
vim.api.nvim_set_keymap('n', ',', [[:<C-u>lua MiniJump.jump(nil, not MiniJump.state.backward)<CR>]], { noremap = true })
vim.api.nvim_set_keymap('n', ',', [[:<C-u>lua MiniJump.smart_jump(not MiniJump.state.backward)<CR>]], { noremap = true })
```
This wouldn't work, as it will just get stuck in a loop, since [`update_state`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e83ea73d13/lua/mini/jump.lua#L425-L441) will be reusing state for subsequent jumps.

However, the following two mappings
```lua
vim.api.nvim_set_keymap('n', ',', [[:<C-u>lua MiniJump.jump(nil, true)<CR>]], { noremap = true })
vim.api.nvim_set_keymap('n', ',', [[:<C-u>lua MiniJump.smart_jump(true)<CR>]], { noremap = true })
```
kinda work, but they would break switch to `;`. So in general, `,` should be considered in a sense of reversing direction of jumps. For instance:
* Instead of using `,,,` (go 3 times backwards) it is better to do `,;;` (`,` -> reverse direction and then `;;` repeat 2 jumps in that reversed direction). 
* Then if you over jumped backwards again, you would need to do `,` to start going forward and however many times `;` to keep going forward, i.e. repeating jumps.

Note, that if you just use `,,,` then you lose ability to go forward without re-initiating search with `f`, as `;` will just continue to go to the reversed direction.

Since this is not ideal, so there is a need for wrapper. Here is what I came up with.
```lua
local M = {}

function M.repeat_in_oposite_direction()
  local state = {}
  for k, v in pairs(MiniJump.state) do
    state[k] = v
  end
  MiniJump.smart_jump(not MiniJump.state.backward)
  MiniJump.state = state
end

vim.api.nvim_set_keymap('n', ',', [[:<C-u>lua require("<this-module>").repeat_in_oposite_direction()<CR>]], { noremap = true })

return M
```
This seems to work with `f` and `F` just fine, and it will also replicate revert in opposite directions for `t` or `T` like in the plain (N)Vim config. But assume that you do `to;;;` which will stop as shown below
```
aaaa o aaaaa o aaaa o aaaa o
    ^       ^      ^      ^
```
But if you over jump and want to go backwards, it will stop after `o`
```
aaaa o aaaaa o aaaa o aaaa o
      ^       ^      ^      ^
```
whereas, I'd like it to just go backwards of the same positions. However, I guess this is outside of scope of this plugin.

```lua

  MiniJump.state.backward = not MiniJump.state.backward
  MiniJump.smart_jump()
  MiniJump.state.backward = not MiniJump.state.backward
end
```

> However, I guess this is outside of scope of this plugin.

It is indeed, yes.

Ironically, original author of module [wasn't a fan of this option](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/pull/8#issuecomment-960606050). My motivation behind this was twofold:

reply_data.bodyHTML:
Thanks for kind words!

What is the easiest way to map mini.ai function_call mapping to something other than f. Is this the only way to do this?

Your example setup already uses c to select function call (based on Lua patterns; allows alphanumeric, underscore, and dot to be inside function name) and f to select function definition (based on tree-sitter).

Alternatively, you can use tree-sitter to select function call (has both pros and cons), which can be achieved with this:

local gen_spec = require('mini.ai').gen_spec
require('mini.ai').setup({
  custom_textobjects = {
    c = gen_spec.treesitter({ a = '@call.outer', i = '@call.inner' }),
    f = gen_spec.treesitter({ a = '@function.outer', i = '@function.inner' }),
  },
})

reply_data.bodyHTML:
Came here looking for a surround option for Markdown code blocks, does this handle newlines?

It can be made to, because new lines are respected (with a caveat).

I would do that by creating (in config directory) a 'after/filetype/markdown/lua' file with the following content:

vim.b.minisurround_config = {
  custom_surroundings = {
    c = { input = { '```\n().-()\n```' }, output = { left = '```\n', right = '\n```' } },
  },
}

The caveat here is that this will work only if first line has zero indent. If not, ``` will be inserted after that indent and the first line in code block will have zero indent. Not sure if this will change, as it works for majority of cases.

Hello! Thanks!

Adding surrounding is done in three steps:
- Initiate "Add surrounding" action via `sa`.
- Tell what region you want to surround via textobject or motion. For example, in your example it can be "around `"`"  which is `a"`.
- Tell which surrounding you want to add via pressing single character surrounding identifier. For a function call, it is `f`. It will prompt you to insert function name: type it (if I understood correctly, you want `W` as a function name) and hit `<CR>` (Enter).

So, overall sequence on characters you need to press is: `saa"fW<CR>` (`<CR>` is single hit on `Enter`). This will result into following state:

```
a := W(|"some_string")
``` 

I am not sure I have 100% understanding of your question, though. Does this help you figure it out?

Here are [some other examples](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/doc/mini-surround.txt#L63).

I used https://github.com/jiangmiao/auto-pairs and https://github.com/tmsvg/pear-tree before with Vim and I prefer the latter as its default behavior makes more sense to me.

comment_data.bodyHTML:
The only "rules" 'mini.pairs' supports is conditioning on cursor's neighborhood. So you can set up to insert pair only if cursor's neighborhood matches some two-character neigh_pattern Lua pattern. You can do this either inside config for built-in characters or inside MiniPairs.map() for manual mapping.

You case is thus can be supported with this setup:

require('mini.pairs').setup({
  mappings = {
    ['"'] = { neigh_pattern = '[^\\]%W' },
  }
})

Here it will insert "" only if previous character is not a \ and next character is not an alphanumeric character. See here for more special Lua patterns.

reply_data.body:
I usually use it like this:
- If I need to save a new session, I do indeed type `:lua MiniSessions.write('new_session')`. This happens not so often, so I don't have mapping for that.
- If I need to read session, at least 99% of the time it is listed in Starter buffer. If not, I type `:lua MiniSessions.select()` and it provides an interface to read any of the detected sessions. It can be used not only to read, but to (re)write and delete. See [its help](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/doc/mini-sessions.txt#L190).

Couple of things worth mentioning:
- The 'mini.sessions' is basically a convenience wrapper for Neovim's built-in sessions mechanism. See `:h mksession` and `:h sessionoptions`.
- You can tell 'mini.sessions' about where to store non-local session files with `directory` option. I have it like this: `require('mini.sessions').setup({ directory = '~/.config/nvim/misc/sessions' })`

reply_data.body:
Hi!

> The docs says "Pairs get automatically registered to be recognized by `<BS>` and `<CR>`". What does this mean?

Typing `<BS>` (backspace) in Insert mode will delete whole pair if it is registered. Like in case of `(|)` (`|` - cursor) it will remove both `(` and `)`. See [`:h MiniPairs.bs()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/doc/mini-pairs.txt#L260).

Typing `<CR>` (enter) in Insert mode will put "close" symbol on next line. Like in case of `(|)` it will create three lines: `(`, `  `, and `)` (second one depends on how your indentation is set up). See [`:h MiniPairs.cr()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/doc/mini-pairs.txt#L273)

> My use case is to use either `<CR>` or `<BS>` to jump to the end of the pair in insert mode.

Both `<CR>` and `<BS>` will be used in 'mini.pairs' only like described above. For you functionality in Normal mode try `:h %`.

comment_data.bodyHTML:
In my previous statusline (lualine), I used something like this to display a clock:

 sections = {
    lualine_y = {'os.date("%H:%M", os.time())'}
  }

Do you think I can have this in ministatusline ? I tried to read the help file, but I don't understand it 🫣

reply_data.body:
'mini.statusline' takes a function-oriented approach to defining statusline. Instead of fixed table with a,b,c,x,y,z sections, it is encouraged to modify [function for default content](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/41023bb1de7e8cf973ae9cf3066e01f3c8f3617d/doc/mini-statusline.txt#L77) to suit your liking. It offers vastly greater flexibility, both in terms of content and its highlighting.

Your setup can be implemented like this:
```lua
require('mini.statusline').setup({
  content = {
    active = function()
      local mode, mode_hl = MiniStatusline.section_mode({ trunc_width = 120 })
      local git           = MiniStatusline.section_git({ trunc_width = 75 })
      local diagnostics   = MiniStatusline.section_diagnostics({ trunc_width = 75 })
      local filename      = MiniStatusline.section_filename({ trunc_width = 140 })
      local time          = os.date("%H:%M", os.time())
      local fileinfo      = MiniStatusline.section_fileinfo({ trunc_width = 120 })
      local location      = MiniStatusline.section_location({ trunc_width = 75 })

      return MiniStatusline.combine_groups({
        { hl = mode_hl,                  strings = { mode } },
        { hl = 'MiniStatuslineDevinfo',  strings = { git, diagnostics } },
        '%<', -- Mark general truncate point
        { hl = 'MiniStatuslineFilename', strings = { filename } },
        '%=', -- End left alignment
        { hl = 'MoreMsg',                strings = { time } },
        { hl = 'MiniStatuslineFileinfo', strings = { fileinfo } },
        { hl = mode_hl,                  strings = { location } },
      })
    end,
  },
})
```

Put table with `{ time }` in place you would like it to be. Choose or define other highlight group you would like it to be.

reply_data.body:
> How do I add nerd font icons in mini.starter and preserve the prefix shortcuts?

Unfortunately, there is no easy way to do this. The 'mini.starter' was intentionally designed to be slightly skewed for easy setup in some default cases at cost of not-so-easy setup in others. This is the latter case.

The designed approach to solve this is to write custom content hook. I'd suggested tweaking the following:

```lua
local pad = string.rep(' ', 22)

-- A content hook to add icons as separate content unit to not disrupt query
--stylua: ignore start
local new_icon_unit = function(icon) return { type = 'icon', string = pad .. icon .. '  ', hl = 'String' } end
local icon_units = {
  ['Find file']    = new_icon_unit(''),
  ['Recent files'] = new_icon_unit(''),
  ['Grep text']    = new_icon_unit(''),
  ['Config']       = new_icon_unit(''),
  ['Lazy']         = new_icon_unit(''),
  ['New file']     = new_icon_unit(''),
  ['Quit']         = new_icon_unit(''),
}
local hook_add_icons = function(content)
  for _, line in ipairs(content) do
    -- If hook is applied first, then item is first content unit in line
    local item = line[1].item
    if item ~= nil then table.insert(line, 1, icon_units[item.name]) end
  end
  return content
end

local starter = require('mini.starter')
local new_section =
  function(name, action, section) return { name = name, action = action, section = pad .. section } end

local config = {
  evaluate_single = true,
  header = logo,
  items = {
    new_section("Find file",    "Telescope find_files", "Telescope"),
    new_section("Recent files", "Telescope oldfiles",   "Telescope"),
    new_section("Grep text",    "Telescope live_grep",  "Telescope"),
    new_section("Config",       "e $MYVIMRC",           "Config"),
    new_section("Lazy",         "Lazy",                 "Config"),
    new_section("New file",     "ene | startinsert",    "Built-in"),
    new_section("Quit",         "qa",                   "Built-in"),
  },
  content_hooks = {
    hook_add_icons,
    starter.gen_hook.aligning("center", "center"),
  },
}
--stylua: ignore end

starter.setup(config)
```

> I'm having trouble figuring out how to change the colors of statusline. Could you give a quick pointer please? I understand how to make new sections but can't figure out how to change the highlight groups for existing default sections or custom ones. 

Highlighting for default sections is controlled by [custom set of highlight groups](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2b37c5e1d2a3f62ba4060a819f17d8d976018928/doc/mini-statusline.txt#L44). You can change them using Neovim's functionality: either with `:highlight` command (see `:h hi`) or with `vim.api.nvim_set_hl()` function using 0 as namespace index (see `:h nvim_set_hl()`.

The most straightforward way to use custom highlighting in new sections is to create new highlight group (using any of the two previous methods) and use it inside `MiniStatusline.combine_groups()`, like in [this example](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2b37c5e1d2a3f62ba4060a819f17d8d976018928/doc/mini-statusline.txt#L77).

> I'm trying to use the starter plugin but when configuring the recent files section like this starter.sections.recent_files(5, true), the plugin claims that "There are no recent files", even though (for instance) Telescope shows multiple old files. Without the true it shows 5 files but not only from the current workdir. Is this to be expected?

Are you sure that there indeed are recent files from **current working directory**. That is, when you execute `:=vim.v.oldfiles`, it does show files from current working directory (which you can see with `:=vim.fn.getcwd()`). If `starter.sections.recent_files(5, false)` works and shows files, then it might be either a misunderstanding on if there are indeed any "current working directory files" or 'mini.starter' doesn't correctly recognize those.

Just for full information, what OS are you using?

> Also, would it be possible to use bracketed to jump to the next / previous git changes?

The suggested solution is to use [lewis6991/gitsigns.nvim](https://github.com/lewis6991/gitsigns.nvim#keymaps) functionality.

> Sorry, also for tabs :)

It is rather straightforward to get 99% there with custom mappings:

```
vim.keymap.set('n', ']t', '<Cmd>tabnext<CR>')
vim.keymap.set('n', '[t', '<Cmd>tabprevious<CR>')
vim.keymap.set('n', ']T', '<Cmd>tablast<CR>')
vim.keymap.set('n', '[T', '<Cmd>tabfirst<CR>')
```

Make sure to also set `config.treesitter.suffix` to `''` for 'mini.bracketed' to not override those or use different suffix for tabpage mappings.

reply_data.body:
If I understand correctly how 'chrisgrieser/nvim-various-textobjs' works, then you can have both it and 'mini.ai' co-exist without *too* much trouble.

The way 'mini.ai' works is by [creating three sets of mappings](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/801627023acf3c41293ac321a43de009076ba037/lua/mini/ai.lua#L1137-L1149) in both Visual and Operator-pending modes: `a`/`i` for regular textobjects, `al`/`il` for "last textobject", `an`/`in` for "next textobject.

If you want to use other Visual and/or Operator-pending mappings that start with `a` or `i`, you can make them ahead but type each key within at most 'timeoutlen' milliseconds apart (see `:h 'timeoutlen'`). Judging by a quick inspection of 'nvim-various-textobject', it creates separate mappings for its textobjects, so this would work.

Now, the tricky part in your question is to use specifically `an` and `in` for "number" textobject. It means to either use different mapping for "next" 'mini.ai' textobject (see [this config settings](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/801627023acf3c41293ac321a43de009076ba037/doc/mini-ai.txt#L411-L412)) or different left hand side for 'nvim-various-textobject' mappings. They can not coexist with default keys.

------

That being said, I think all various textobjects from 'nvim-various-textobjects' can be replicated within 'mini.ai' specification at least to a certain degree (where only workflow can slightly vary).

I can't see a way to fully replicate `number` textobject from 'nvim-various-textobject' (judging by [this code](https://github.com/chrisgrieser/nvim-various-textobjs/blob/2bfacdaa18c1be9db83a88bce7def12295850ecd/lua/various-textobjs/charwise-textobjs.lua#L243-L252)). This is mostly because 'mini.ai' is designed assuming each "a" textobject contains only one "i" textobject, while the cases like `-123.456` can have two "inner number"s based on 'nvim-various-textobject' definition.

I would suggest using slightly different approach with the following "digits" textobject:
```lua
require('mini.ai').setup({
  custom_textobjects = {
    -- "Digits" textobject. Matches consecutive digits possibly prefixed by
    -- `-` or `.`. This allows selecting on both sides of decimal point,
    -- possibly with consecutive application.
    -- NOTE: `a` and `i` textobjects select same regions.
    --
    -- Example. Place cursor inside all of numbers, press `v`, and keep
    -- hitting `id` until possible:
    --   123 -123 123.456 -123.456
    d = { '[%-%.]?%f[%d]%d+' },
  },
})
```

reply_data.body:
> Is there alternatives for the `lineCharacterwise` objects / motions?

Yes, writing your own. Something like this:
```lua
require('mini.ai').setup({
  custom_textobjects = {
    L = function(ai_type)
      local line_num = vim.fn.line('.')
      local line = vim.fn.getline(line_num)
      -- Select `\n` past the line for `a` to delete it whole
      local from_col, to_col = 1, line:len() + 1
      if ai_type == 'i' then
        if line:len() == 0 then
          -- Don't remove empty line
          from_col, to_col = 0, 0
        else
          -- Ignore indentation for `i` textobject and don't remove `\n` past the line
          from_col = line:match('^%s*()')
          to_col = line:len()
        end
      end

      return { from = { line = line_num, col = from_col }, to = { line = line_num, col = to_col } }
    end,
  },
})
```

reply_data.body:
> can't be all lsp candidates be filtered through mini.fuzzy automatically?

Not really.

When completion is initiated in 'mini.completion', it first computes candidates from LSP and processes them using `lsp_completion.process_items`. After that, filtering is done through Neovim's built-in completion methods which are not fuzzy. So in order to leverage fuzzy matching from 'mini.fuzzy' after having entered some number of characters, extra call to LSP is needed for `lsp_completion.process_items` (that is, fuzzy matching from 'mini.fuzzy') to take effect.

reply_data.body:
Hi!

> Essentially I would just like to select everything inside of the nearest matching pair of {}, <>, [], "", '', () and be able to combine that selection with yank/delete/whatever else in my own keymaps.

Yes, this does sound like the job for 'mini.ai' in particular and textobjects in general (see `:h text-objects`). What you'd generally do is one of two approaches:
- First visually select the region and then apply action (via built-in or custom Visual mode mapping). So to delete inside matching `()`: `vi)` followed by `d`.
- Use operator to perform its action on textobject. It is either built-in ones (`y`, `d`, `c`, etc.; see `:h operator`) or by manually created ones (like `gc` from 'mini.comment'). So deleting inside `()` now becomes `di)`.

The operator approach is slightly less intuitive but has its benefits: 1) less keystrokes; 2) dot-repeatable (type `di)` and then press `.` when inside another parenthesis); 3) doesn't affect latest visual selection.

Does this help or you have something else in mind?

reply_data.body:
:wave:

First of all, to answer your question on hand:
- `<C-S-f>` can have problems with being a left hand side of a mapping (if even able to work). This has to do with how terminal emulators recognize key modifiers: `Ctrl+<key>` is usually ok, but `Ctrl+Shift+<key>` usually not. So be careful with using it.
- 'mini.align' doesn't have `start()` function. It has [`align_user()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/f2b89efbbad1943657e43f474fe308fceb63597e/doc/mini-align.txt#L574) which, to be honest, not really user-friendly when it comes to using in custom mappings.
- **If** you really want a mapping to automatically start aligning inner paragraph, I'd recommend going with something like this:
    ```lua
    vim.keymap.set('n', '<C-S-f>', 'gaip', { remap = true })
    ```
    This basically emulates key presses 'g', 'a', 'i', 'p' as if user typed them (thanks to `remap = true`). Here `ga` should be one of the defined in [`config.mappings`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/f2b89efbbad1943657e43f474fe308fceb63597e/doc/mini-align.txt#L431-L432). So having `gA` also possible which will start interactive aligning.

**But** my honest suggestion would be to not make these kind of mappings and start getting comfortable with using textobjects (the `ip` bit meaning "inner paragraph") and dot-repeat (you can press `gaip` to align one paragraph only later needing to press `.` to repeat that edit; if no other editing was done, of course).

comment_data.body: Hello, sorry for asking i'm quite new with neovim and stuff, may i ask how does mini.bufremove work? does it override the neovims :bd? or do i need to use the Mini.bufremove.delete() function in order to use it?
comment_data.bodyHTML: Hello, sorry for asking i'm quite new with neovim and stuff, may i ask how does mini.bufremove work? does it override the neovims :bd? or do i need to use the Mini.bufremove.delete() function in order to use it?
comment_data.bodyText: Hello, sorry for asking i'm quite new with neovim and stuff, may i ask how does mini.bufremove work? does it override the neovims :bd? or do i need to use the Mini.bufremove.delete() function in order to use it?

reply_data.body:
Hi! Welcome to Neovim world!

It exports (provides for the user) several functions which will remove certain buffer. So no, it doesn't override `:bd` and friends.

Typical usage is to create mappings for common actions. Here is essentially what I use:

```lua
-- Not strictly needed.
-- If omitted, use `require('mini.bufremove')` in mappings instead of `MiniBufremove`
require('mini.bufremove').setup()

local nmap_leader = function(keys, rhs, desc)
  vim.keymap.set('n', '<Leader>' .. suffix, rhs, { desc = desc })
end

nmap_leader('bd', '<Cmd>lua MiniBufremove.delete()<CR>',         'Delete buffer')
nmap_leader('bD', '<Cmd>lua MiniBufremove.delete(0,  true)<CR>', 'Delete! buffer')

nmap_leader('bw', '<Cmd>lua MiniBufremove.wipeout()<CR>',        'Wipeout buffer')
nmap_leader('bW', '<Cmd>lua MiniBufremove.wipeout(0, true)<CR>', 'Wipeout! buffer')
```

But mostly I use only `MiniBufremove.wipeout()`. For difference between "delete buffer" and "wipeout buffer" see `:h :bdelete` and `:h :bwipeout`.

Alternatively, you can manually wipeout buffer by typing `:lua require('mini.bufremove').wipeout()` and follow with `<CR>` (`<Enter>`).

TIL "OptionSet", thank!

---@type LazyPluginSpec
return {
  ---@diagnostic disable-next-line: assign-type-mismatch
  {
    [[f-person/auto-dark-mode.nvim]],
    event = [[VeryLazy]],
    dependencies = {
      {
        [[echasnovski/mini.colors]],
        config = function()
          local MiniColors = require [[mini.colors]]
          MiniColors.setup()
          vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd(
            [[OptionSet]],
            {
              pattern = [[background]],
              callback = function()
                -- HACK: Cache the correct state first and then enforce the
                -- opposite state before transitioning rigth back to the
                -- correct one.
                --
                vim.o.background = (vim.o.background == [[light]]) and [[dark]] or [[light]]
                local cs = { MiniColors.get_colorscheme() or {} }
                vim.o.background = (vim.o.background == [[light]]) and [[dark]] or [[light]]
                MiniColors.animate(cs, {
                  transition_steps = 100
                })
              end
            })
        end
      }
    },

    ---@diagnostic disable-next-line: assign-type-mismatch
    config = {
      -- HACK: To prevent conflict, we need to be clever when setting
      -- vim.o.background in our OptionSet cmd. The strategy here is to invert
      -- the logic to ensure they don't cancel each other out.
      --
      set_dark_mode = function()
        vim.o.background = [[light]]
      end,
      set_light_mode = function()
        vim.o.background = [[dark]]
      end
    }
  }
}

reply_data.body:
>     1. `mini.ai` has the `g]` and `g[` to go to the textobject, but I can't use `.`, `,` or `;` to repeat. Is it a good idea to support so?

Dot-repeat is supported only for commands that edit text, as it is described in `:h .`. So movement (except some early design mismatch in 'mini.surround') and visual selection is not supported with `.`.

`,` and `;` are reserved for repeating `fFtT` motions, so also will not be supported.

>     2. Similar question. `mini.surround` has commands that don't support repeat. For example, if after `vi(`  I hit `i(`  it will select the next match, but is it more convenient to use `.`, `,` or `;`? `di(` however supports repeat by hitting `.`.

`i(` is the textobject from 'mini.ai', not a functionality from 'mini.surround'. So the answer is similar to previous one.
The `i(` in Visual mode expanding selection is a "consecutive application" feature which allows exactly that.

>     3. My `mini.hipatterns` (in above link) uses the config from the example. It shows an underline in the pattern words, but no highlight (screenshot below). I don't know much about the highlight groups, but I assume those like `MiniHipatternsFixme` are auto-installed by the plugin?  I'm using  `gruvbox-material` theme.

Those use [supplied highlight groups](https://github.com/xixiaofinland/dotfiles/blob/34875fb29894eaf0009fb74305edac75e064c72e/.config/nvim/lua/plugins/mini.lua#L54-L57). Those particular ones are indeed created by 'mini.hipatterns' inside its `setup()` and by default are [linked to `Diagnostic*` groups](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/ea1af8c7d5e72148cae8a04e9887322a53fe66cf/lua/mini/hipatterns.lua#L711-L714). I'd assume those are defined same as you describe. You can look by executing two commands: `:hi MiniHipatternsFixme` and `:hi DiagnosticError`.

If you want to tweak them, take a look at how highlight groups work. Start with `:h highlight`.

comment_data.body: In `mini.pick` module, how do I change the windows `winblend`? And, how can I disable a mapping (it was not specified in the docs)?
comment_data.bodyHTML: In mini.pick module, how do I change the windows winblend? And, how can I disable a mapping (it was not specified in the docs)?
comment_data.bodyText: In mini.pick module, how do I change the windows winblend? And, how can I disable a mapping (it was not specified in the docs)?

reply_data.body:
> In `mini.pick` module, how do I change the windows `winblend`?

Either set global `'winblend'` (which is used by default) or modify window's `'winblend'` when the window is created. The most straightforward way to do this is inside [autocommand  for dedicated event](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/ea1af8c7d5e72148cae8a04e9887322a53fe66cf/doc/mini-pick.txt#L140) like this:
```lua
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', {
  pattern = 'MiniPickStart',
  callback = function()
    local win_id = MiniPick.get_picker_state().windows.main
    vim.wo[win_id].winblend = 0
  end,
})
```

> And, how can I disable a mapping (it was not specified in the docs)?

Override with different key which is not reachable via custom key query process. For example, empty string. Something like this:
```lua
require('mini.pick').setup({ mappings = { toggle_preview = '' } })
```

Out of curiosity, which mapping do you need to disable and why?

reply_data.body:
> I guess I just prefer freeing up some keys for who knows why haha!

Well, default values of all those mappings are not usable as part of prompt (they all use modifier like `Ctrl` or `Alt`). And all mappings are only valid when picker window is open and custom key process is active. So removing them have no effect outside of active picker.

The only valid reason I see for disabling them is to *make sure* that nothing happens if those are pressed by mistake.

reply_data.body:
Hi, Xiao!

That's an admirable goal, for sure! My first (and probably the most important one) is to make sure that what you do brings you joy. Chances are that plugin development won't directly translate into a serious line in the resume. I'd say that main takeaways are general programming practice, better understanding of your programming tools (Neovim and its plugins) and potential GitHub/Neovim/Lua social contacts. Be sure that is ok with you.

About actual plugin development... There are quite a few practices that can be followed but usually none is "the only true one". What I can share are some bits of advice that *I* feel strongly about and I think every plugin should follow:
- Read documentation. A lot. You can start with `:h intro`, first sections of `:h windows`, and relevant (to you) sections of `:h api`.
- Have proper help in Vim format. That is, a file 'doc/myplugin.txt' which is formatted to be shown as `help` fieltype with tags for core searchable topics (general description, function names, etc.). See `:h helphelp` for more.
    I prefer to write this documentation in a single file as EmmyLua comments and ended up writing 'mini.doc' to convert them. But those can be written separately and manually.
- Have tests. Prior to writing/using 'mini.nvim', absence of tests was a *very* strong indicator that I should not use the plugin.
    Again, I ended up writing and extensively using 'mini.test', but [test harness in 'plenary.nvim'](https://github.com/nvim-lua/plenary.nvim#plenarytest_harness) is a popular choice. Or straight up [busted](https://github.com/lunarmodules/busted), but this is tricky.
- Read about Lua as a language (`:h lua` or [learn x in y minutes for Lua](https://learnxinyminutes.com/docs/lua/)).
- Read and try to understand source code of popular plugins and Neovim itself. I don't say follow everything you see, but understanding why something is done will help you decide if you want to follow some conventions.
- Find place with like minded people to ask questions. At the moment, this place for Neovim seems to be [its Matrix room](https://app.element.io/#/room/#neovim:matrix.org) and [Neovim subreddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/neovim/), but I might be missing others.

I wish you well in this journey. If you have any specific/targeted questions, I'll try to answer them (just maybe not immediately).

Not really. Try getting used to the fact that `il'` and `al'` are separate textobjects in their own right while `2i'` and `2a'` are "extensions" of that textobjects.

comment_data.bodyText:
mini.jump2d
Is there a way to configure jump2d to only spot certain LSP symbols? For example, I would like to spot only (the first character of) variables and function calls in my code.
If not that, is there a way to configure builtin_opts.word_start to not consider _ as word separator? Basically, I would like it if word_start uses Vim's definition of a "word"
Thanks!

reply_data.body:
'mini.jump2d' operates on the concept of [spotter function](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/1cd8d7e8318071eddc536815f5cafe50b012ac29/doc/mini-jump2d.txt#L202-L219), which in theory can be used to spot any places with a reasonable system behind them.

That said, doing it for LSP symbols will be kind of not trivial.

> Basically, I would like it if `word_start` uses Vim's definitaion of a "word"

This is not really trivial as it sounds, because what is considered to be a "word" is conditioned on 'iskeyword' option. But this is doable with Vim's regex, as there is a '\k' character class which matches any keyword character.

> If not that, is there a way to configure `builtin_opts.word_start` to not consider `_` as word separator?

Assuming only Latin characters, this is the most doable quickly. It can be done with [`gen_pattern_spotter()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/1cd8d7e8318071eddc536815f5cafe50b012ac29/doc/mini-jump2d.txt#L339). So jumping can be started with this command: `MiniJump2d.start({ spotter = MiniJump2d.gen_pattern_spotter('[%w_]+') })`. You can either use set a default spotter or make a mapping with that command.

Basically, [the intro](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/d1413e1cacaacd29e420b9482754e762076e64ac/doc/mini-doc.txt#L9-L31) contains the big picture of how 'mini.doc' operates. That is:
- Process single file from top to bottom and convert *every* `---` block (which starts at first column) into a section in corresponding help file (which are delimited by long `----------` lines).
- Process files in order and merge them with long `==========` lines.

Other than that, I'd advise to open a source `.lua` file with its corresponding `.txt` help file and see how things are done. For example, ['mini/comment.lua'](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/lua/mini/comment.lua) and ['mini-comment.txt'](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/doc/mini-comment.txt).

Blocked child process is a common problem of testing with child process. It usually indicates that it expects some user input. The most common causes for me are:
- Hit-enter-prompt (see `:h hit-enter-prompt`). Usually because of a long message shown in Command line (increasing `cmdheight` can help here) or errors (with or without long message).
- Operator-pending mode. Like when test simulated a `d` key which blocks everything and waits for user input. Sending the keys with `child.type_keys()` which stops Operator-pending mode usually solves this.

Other than that, blocked child process is solved on a case by case basis. Usually by trial and error of bisecting plugin and/or test code, or trying to manually simulate what test does and see what causes it.

end

In `minimal_init.lua` in [README](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/TESTING.md), there is `if #vim.api.nvim_list_uis() == 0`, but it is a table rather than `0` in headless nvim too. Not at all. You'd have to design a mock yourself. Some my current approach at mocking this type of thing is roughly this:

```lua
_G.jobstart_log = {}

vim.fn.jobstart = function(...)
  table.insert(_G.jobstart_log, { ... })
  -- Emulate `jobstart()` behavior as closely as you need for your plugin to work
end
```

Later check that `_G.jobstart_log` is the same as you'd expect: `eq(child.lua_get('_G.jobstart_log'), ref_jobstart_log)`. This is not perfect as it makes tests depend on implementation (for example, changing order of `jobstart()` calls might not matter to the actual result but tests would need to be updated), but works good enough for me right now.

> Hello, thanks for your plugins.

:pray:

> It seems that the mini-clue doesn't expose extra functions to register clues?
> 
> How can I only append clues in certain cases, for example, when lsp clients are attached?

The only way to configure clues in 'mini.clue' is by setting/updating [`config.clues`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/16600082b7b3e3ee3aa3d59f2bc589fc60ffcada/doc/mini-clue.txt#L516).

"Dynamic" clues is not really a use case that 'mini.clue' is designed for. One way to implement this would be to have an autocommands for `LspAttach` and `LspDetach` inside which `MiniClue.config.clues` is modified directly to fit your use case.

reply_data.body:
> Thanks for all of your work 👍

Thanks for using it :pray:

>     1. How to hide the status line on the starter page? There are examples in the readme, but they didnt work me. I tried several auto commands and ftplugins to no avail.

The suggested approach is to use autocommand black magic. As 'mini.starter' is somewhat special (obligated to have maximum performance), it disables any autocommands when it is created. In exchange, it [provides its own `MiniStarterOpened` `User` event](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/78a4d457718060fe80480c72a7d64f6b23472d63/doc/mini-starter.txt#L262) for users to utilize.
So eventually something like this should work:

```lua
local disable_statusline = function(data) vim.b[data.buf].ministatusline_disable = true end
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', { pattern = 'MiniStarterOpened', callback = disable_statusline })
require('mini.starter').setup()
```

It would still technically *show* statusline, albeit consisting from empty line. If you want to fully *hide* it, then some more autocommand black magic is needed:

```lua
local temp_disable_statusline = function(au_data)
  vim.o.laststatus = 0
  local au_opts = { buffer = au_data.buf, once = true, callback = function() vim.o.laststatus = 2 end }
  vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('BufLeave', au_opts)
end
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', { pattern = 'MiniStarterOpened', callback = temp_disable_statusline })
require('mini.starter').setup()
```
 
>     2. How to add "slanted" design to the status line components? I tried several ways but couldn't get it to work correctly. I need a way to add a character between two components and for this character invert the foreground/background color.

All sections in 'mini.statusline' are plain functions which return strings. It is left to user to combine them however they want. [Here is how it is done by default](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/78a4d457718060fe80480c72a7d64f6b23472d63/doc/mini-statusline.txt#L81-L98). For the most common case of combining groups, there is [`combine_groups()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/78a4d457718060fe80480c72a7d64f6b23472d63/doc/mini-statusline.txt#L161) which is a bit smarter version of plain string concatenation. Outside of that it is expected to manipulate section strings manually.

As I haven't really had experience with those type of section separators (as I don't really like how they look), unfortunately that's all I can help you with right now. Hope it helps.

It looks like you want to open 'tex' file for editing? If yes, then this body of custom `choose` should already work:

				if filetype.detect(item.text) == "pdf" then

					return
				end
				MiniPick.default_choose(item)
```

If you want to preview the file in picker's window, then press `<Tab>` and it should work as is.

Yes, there is and it is quite a Vim way, dare I say :)

The `builtin.grep` source [accepts `pattern` option](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/c3b37f4afb933141a750b60b86fb6ef6b50d0e61/doc/mini-pick.txt#L1078-L1079). reply_data.body:
Hi! Thanks for kind words!

> I've been digging around some threads but can't find a way to select a comment block with some combination of `mini.comment` or `mini.ai`. Is this possible?
> 
> I can delete a block with dgc and toggle it with gcgc, so I figured I could do vgc or do something like vagc, but it doesn't do what I expected it to do. My idea of how text objects work may very well be incorrect though!

Your idea of how textobject work is generally on point. It does not, however, work exactly like that with the [default config](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e025ee74705b04dd25a132a521c9c535dc78a8d8/doc/mini-comment.txt#L87-L102) of 'mini.comment'.

The *cause* of this is that `gc` in Visual mode (when visual selection is active) toggles comments on selected lines and not acts as "select textobject". In turn, `gc` acts as textobject in Operator-pending mode (as in `dgc` to delete comment block or even `gcgc` to uncomment current comment block).

The *reason* of this design is that visually selecting textobject is rarely the end goal. Comment block is usually needed to be acted upon: delete, change, yank, uncomment, etc. Hence it is set up only in Operator-pending mode by default.

Some more traditional commenting plugins overcome this by using different keys for toggling comments in Visual mode, but this looks a bit confusing to be default. However, since [a bit over a month ago](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/commit/79b1b3350f1cac7cef9e46a637f9adf2a14b4923) it is now possible to set up visual selection of comment block as textobject by having different keys for `mappings.comment_visual` and `mappings.textobject`. For example:

```lua
require('mini.comment').setup({ mappings = { comment_visual = 'C' } })
```

Now pressing `vgc` will select current comment block and pressing `C` in Visual mode will toggle comments.

reply_data.body:
Unfortunately, I don't think there is a way to do that. 'mini.pairs' is design to work **only** for a two-character neighborhoods and pairs.

My best suggestion would be to enable "open" (or "closeopen", you choice) pairs for both `%` and ` ` inside target filetype plugins (in 'after/ftplugin/xxx.lua' files) with something like this:

```lua
if _G.MiniPairs ~= nil then
  MiniPairs.map_buf(0, 'i', '%', { action = 'open', pair = '%%', neigh_pattern = '{}' })
  MiniPairs.map_buf(0, 'i', ' ', { action = 'open', pair = '  ', neigh_pattern = '%%' })
end
```

So now typing `{% ` inserts `{%  %}`. But otherwise should insert only a single character each.

reply_data.body:
I happened to have this already in my config. Here's how I set it up:

Inside of either `ftplugin/python.lua` or `after/ftplugin/python.lua`, you can use:
```lua
require("mini.pairs").map_buf(0, "i", "'", {
  action = "closeopen",
  pair = "''",
  neigh_pattern = "[^A-Za-eg-z\\].",
  register = { cr = false } },
})
```
This is just a slight modification of the default `'` pair rule from the `mini.pairs` documentation, so it should behave the same everywhere _except_ immediately after a lowercase "f".

reply_data.bodyHTML:
I, too, find it a bit unergonomic if I have to type :lua anything in my daily workflow. And, to be honest, I was a bit surprised to see there was no equivalent MiniSessions.save() that would prompt me. I thought I misread the docs as I was sure it must exist given so many of the other mini tools have prompts. So, I wrote my own save session function that prompts for a session name with auto-completion of existing sessions.

I use <leader>ql to load a session and <leader>qs to save sessions:

{
    "echasnovski/mini.sessions",
    lazy = false,
    opts = {},
    keys = {
      {
        "<leader>ql",
        function()
          MiniSessions.select()
        end,
        desc = "Load session",
      },
      {
        "<leader>qs",
        function()
          local res = utils.get_session_from_user("Save session as: ")
          if res ~= nil then
            MiniSessions.write(res)
          end
        end,
        desc = "Save session",
      },
    },
  }

And the helper function from my utils. Not sure it makes sense to provide auto-complete here of existing sessions, but why not:

-- Get session name from user
M.get_session_from_user = function(prompt)
  M._session_complete = function(arg_lead)
    return vim.tbl_filter(function(x)
      return x:find(arg_lead, 1, true) ~= nil
    end, vim.tbl_keys(MiniSessions.detected))
  end
  local completion = "customlist,v:lua.KazUtils._session_complete"
  local ok, res = pcall(vim.fn.input, {
    prompt = prompt,
    cancelreturn = false,
    completion = completion,
  })
  if not ok or res == false then
    return nil
  end
  return res
end

In hindsight, not sure why I stuffed the _session_complete inside as I don’t need the closure.

Recent versions of neovim now automatically attempt to set the value of `termguicolors` based on the capabilities of the terminal emulator. This works really well, but there is one thing that I'm struggling with in `mini.basics`.

reply_data.body:
> Unfortunately, this approach always results in `options.extra_ui` being set to `false`, regardless of the value of `termguicolors`. I'm assuming this is because the value of `termguicolors` only gets set after a certain point in startup and therefore always evaluates to `false` at this point?

First what should be mentioned is that 'termguicolors' is automatically set only on current Neovim Nightly (0.10). If you use earlier versions (including current stable release 0.9.5), it is expected to be set manually. If that is the case, make sure that `require('mini.basics').setup()` is called after 'termguicolors' is set during startup.

On Nightly, however, 'termguicolors' indeed is set automagically [after `VimEnter` event](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/26579). So if `require('mini.basics').setup()` is called immediately at startup (which it probably should) and not lazy loaded, then indeed it is too early to get the eventually set 'termguicolors' option value.

My honest recommendation here would be to use `extra_ui = false` and setting [its options](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/decd729b784c4f6cb775da335f3c8eecb846250c/lua/mini/basics.lua#L488-L499) manually inside an autocommand for `OptionSet` event. So with something like this:

```lua
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('OptionSet', {
  pattern = 'termguicolors',
  callback = function()
    -- Set options only if 'termguicolors' is set
    if not vim.o.termguicolors then return end

    vim.o.pumblend = 10 -- Make builtin completion menus slightly transparent
    vim.o.pumheight = 10 -- Make popup menu smaller
    vim.o.winblend = 10 -- Make floating windows slightly transparent

    vim.o.listchars = 'tab:> ,extends:…,precedes:…,nbsp:␣' -- Define which helper symbols to show
    vim.o.list = true -- Show some helper symbols

    -- Enable syntax highlighting if it wasn't already (as it is time consuming)
    if vim.fn.exists('syntax_on') ~= 1 then vim.cmd([[syntax enable]]) end
  end,
})
```

Consider the following example I came up with for a line textobject:

mini_ai.setup({
  custom_textobjects = {
    -- current line/row
    r = function()
      local line = vim.api.nvim_win_get_cursor(0)[1]
      return {
        from = { line = line, col = 1 },
        to = { line = line, col = math.max(vim.fn.getline(line):len(), 1) }
      }
    end,
  }
})

What I want is my from.col to conditionally include leading whitespace depending on whether it's an inside or around motion, much like vim's ^ vs 0 in normal mode. Maybe there's a variable I can check to see which of these textobjects was triggered?

I see examples of doing this with gen_spec for treesitter, but it seems like overkill for what I think is a simple situation.

reply_data.bodyHTML:
The callable form of textobject specification takes same arguments as MiniAi.find_textobject(). For this particular case using only the first one ai_type should allow returning two different regions based on it.

Coincidentally, there is a direct solution to this particular problem in MiniExtra.gen_ai_spec.line(). So either copy paste the code or use it directly in 'mini.ai'. With something like this:

require('mini.extra').setup()
require('mini.ai').setup({
  custom_textobjects = {
    L = MiniExtra.gen_ai_spec.line(),
  },
})

Whether or not `:help` has an entry for specific plugin is decided on presence of help tags there. Those are usually generated with `:helptags` command (see `:h :helptags`).

reply_data.body:
> Hi, I'm curious why mini.surround works differently to other mappings in neovim. Usually I have infinite time to enter all the parts of the command. But with surround I have to be fast and if I miss the timing, it deletes the current character. I'm not sure if this is intended behaviour. Would love to hear why it behaves this way, thanks. :)

There is no "infinite" time to enter a mapping in Neovim as it is limited to `:h timeoutlen`.

So it is not how 'mini.surround' behaves per se, but the fact that it uses "prefix style" mappings `sa` / `sd` / `sr`, etc. If you only press `s` and wait longer than 'timeoutlen' milliseconds, Neovim thinks that you are done entering a mapping and it executes `s` (which deletes a character under cursor, see `:h s`).

There are at least two ways to mitigate this:
- Increase value of 'timeoutlen'.
- Disable `s` key entirely: `vim.keymap.set({ 'n', 'x' }, 's', '<Nop>')`

reply_data.body:
> Hi, I am trying to visually select a comment with `vgc` and it indeed works but it lags for around 1 sec before the visual selection is made.

The delay between finishing typing mapping keys and they actually execute usually is a result of some other similar mappings present. If Neovim is not sure if user has finished typing, it waits for 'timeoutlen' milliseconds (by default 1000, i.e. 1 second) for the new key press. If there is none - it execute the current keys.

In this example, there are two mappings in Visual mode: `gc` (textobject) and `gcc` (toggle comment for visual selection). After you type `vgc`, Neovim does not know if it needs to wait for the next `c` and execute `vgcc` or execute `vgc` right away.

My advice would be to select a different `comment_visual` keys if you want `vgc` to visually select the comment block.

> how do I rewrite this to use `mini.deps` to install `obsidian.nvim` and the `plenary.nvim` dependency?

To install plugin along with some dependencies, use [`depends` field of specification](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/061379f082d6b03305b00ddd6f8f6b7b8eded6d8/doc/mini-deps.txt#L275-L277). Rewriting everything else needs understanding of what those fields mean in 'lazy.nvim' specification. It looks like most of the fields should be transformed into a corresponding calls: like `opts = ...` into `require('xxx').setup(...)`; `keys` - into explicit mappings, and so on.

reply_data.body:
> I open a file in nvim then exit. I assume a local session is stored.

Not quite. The 'mini.sessions' module is designed to work with [built-in concept of sessions](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2d0f10540efdbb1f5c480ebe19ce4de451936a5d/doc/mini-sessions.txt#L15-L16). With default `autowrite = true` it will [write only if there is an active current session](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2d0f10540efdbb1f5c480ebe19ce4de451936a5d/doc/mini-sessions.txt#L34), which there was not, as it requires either `:lua MiniSessions.write('session-name')`, `:lua MiniSessions.read('session-to-read')`, or `:source` of special session file.

So there needs to be a conscious decision to start a session with `:lua MiniSessions.write('session-name')` which will then be used automatically on the next run if `autoread = true`. See also [this comment](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/discussions/33#discussioncomment-4894341) for more information.

reply_data.body:
> I am using the `select_path(nil, { filter = "core" })` to view added paths to this label. How can I configure it to start in the normal mode instead of insert mode?

I am assuming you use `vim.ui.select = MiniPick.ui_select`, right? If this is the case, then 'mini.pick' simply does not have concept of Normal or Insert mode. It implements its own key query process in order to implement "one window UI". Query displayed at the top is not a separate buffer/window, but a window title which is updated after every key press. This design also allows synchronous execution that returns the chosen item.

So I guess the answer here is "unfortunately, there is no way to do that and it is by design".

I am assuming you use vim.ui.select = MiniPick.ui_select, right? If this is the case, then 'mini.pick' simply does not have concept of Normal or Insert mode. It implements its own key query process in order to implement "one window UI". Query displayed at the top is not a separate buffer/window, but a window title which is updated after every key press. This design also allows synchronous execution that returns the chosen item.
So I guess the answer here is "unfortunately, there is no way to do that and it is by design".

I would like to try setting up robust support for tags within jsx/tsx files in mini.surround and mini.ai. My motivation is that I very frequently use surround to e.g. replace the parent HTML element / React component with another one, add a new element wrapping an existing one etc.  

Here is a specific, but simplified, example of an issue I encounter with mini.surround. Let's say I want to replace the div wrapping the two inner divs with a different element:
![image](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/assets/80899692/6398d6c9-0ea5-4c9c-a412-c260a6649277)

Using `sht` inside one of the inner divs will correctly highlight the inner div:
![image](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/assets/80899692/f82ac155-1af2-46b7-8862-fe3f9f78deaf)
![image](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/assets/80899692/c7e9f229-dea4-44a0-a8df-fd85f7258743)

Using `sht` inside the outer div skips one level and highlights the nav above it: 
![image](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/assets/80899692/d1190bf3-6e0f-4f10-92a4-b8f6fab3646b)
![image](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/assets/80899692/78af4d31-72f9-4a22-b36b-c5db36fe1425)

As will using `2sht` inside the inner div. It skips the outer, containing, div straight to nav one level above:
![image](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/assets/80899692/06d71c07-6e76-4e9d-b494-95f534d7f17a)

I am aware of the reply to this [discussion](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/discussions/285) as well as [these](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/issues/755) [three](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/issues/156#issuecomment-1308429031) [issues](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/issues/110#issuecomment-1212277863) regarding nested tags. The recommendation is to go with a tree-sitter based approach. Could I ask for a little help setting up the mini.surround and mini.ai config following that advice? 

Based on the [mini.surround](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e025ee74705b04dd25a132a521c9c535dc78a8d8/doc/mini-surround.txt#L732) and [mini.ai](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e025ee74705b04dd25a132a521c9c535dc78a8d8/doc/mini-ai.txt#L673) documentation (btw. is it intentional that one is `.gen_spec.input.treesitter()` while the other is `gen_spec.treesitter()`?) the setup of a tree-sitter based textobject should go something like this:

Mini.surround
```
  local ts_input = require('mini.surround').gen_spec.input.treesitter
  require('mini.surround').setup({
    custom_textobjects = {
      t = ts_input({ outer = '@call.outer', inner = '@call.inner' }),
    }
  })
```

Mini.ai
```
  local spec_treesitter = require('mini.ai').gen_spec.treesitter
  require('mini.ai').setup({
    custom_textobjects = {
      F = spec_treesitter({ a = '@function.outer', i = '@function.inner' }),
    }
  })
```
I tried specifying `outer` /  `inner` and `a` / `i` a few different ways but with limited success so far.

Here's an `:InspectTree` of a very simple `.tsx` example:
![image](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/assets/80899692/8705fbab-24b1-41ac-a948-84b1f2ed8dad)

If I understood the documentation correctly then the two most common cases should be:

1) An outer `@jsx_element` with one or more inner `@jsx_element`s
```
(jsx_element ; [4, 4] - [7, 10]
  open_tag: (jsx_opening_element ; [4, 4] - [4, 9]
    name: (identifier)) ; [4, 5] - [4, 8]
  (jsx_element ... )
  (jsx_element ... )
  close_tag: (jsx_closing_element ; [7, 4] - [7, 10]
    name: (identifier))) ; [7, 6] - [7, 9]
```
2) An outer `@jsx_element` with an inner `@jsx_text`
```
  (jsx_element ; [5, 6] - [5, 43]
    open_tag: (jsx_opening_element ; [5, 6] - [5, 31]
      name: (identifier) ; [5, 7] - [5, 8]
    (jsx_text) ; [5, 31] - [5, 39]
    close_tag: (jsx_closing_element ; [5, 39] - [5, 43]
      name: (identifier))) ; [5, 41] - [5, 42]
```

How would I accurately represent this in `custom_textobjects`?

reply_data.body:
> Based on the [mini.surround](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e025ee74705b04dd25a132a521c9c535dc78a8d8/doc/mini-surround.txt#L732) and [mini.ai](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e025ee74705b04dd25a132a521c9c535dc78a8d8/doc/mini-ai.txt#L673) documentation (btw. is it intentional that one is `.gen_spec.input.treesitter()` while the other is `gen_spec.treesitter()`?) the setup of a tree-sitter based textobject should go something like this:

Yes, indeed, using tree-sitter textobjects and surroundings is a recommended approach.

Yes, it is intentional that 'mini.surround' has `gen_spec.input` while 'mini.ai' has `gen_spec` directly. The reason for this is that 'mini.surround' [has two parts of surrounding specification](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2833045cbbe6df8cc3affd6767e211b78b6085bd/doc/mini-surround.txt#L257-L261): `input` for defining how surrounding behaves in "input" operations (delete, find; i.e. when surrounding is the object being operated *upon*) and `output` for "output" operations (add and second step of replace; i.e. when surrounding is put in the buffer).

Here is [an example for "(" built-in surrounding](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2833045cbbe6df8cc3affd6767e211b78b6085bd/lua/mini/surround.lua#L1048): for "input" it is a nested pattern for how parenthesis should be found, for "output" - parts which should be put on the left and right of target region.

> ... the setup of a tree-sitter based textobject should go something like this:

The 'mini.ai' example is syntactically correct, while 'mini.surround' one is not, which look like a cope paste error more than anything. Here is [the reference example](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2833045cbbe6df8cc3affd6767e211b78b6085bd/doc/mini-surround.txt#L734-L742). Use `custom_surroundings` instead of `custom_textobjects` and have extra nesting with "input"`.

> How would I accurately represent this in `custom_textobjects`?

In general, the process is [described in help](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2833045cbbe6df8cc3affd6767e211b78b6085bd/doc/mini-ai.txt#L681-L699). It involves having a specific "textobject" query reachable from your setup (help describes how to check it).

You'd have to follow *exactly* the names of captures (things that start with `@`) in some 'textobjects.scm' query file. The easiest way to have those captures defined indeed proved to be installing ['nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter-textobjects'](https://github.com/nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter-textobjects) plugin (just make it reachable from current session, no need to use its functionality).

*This* is where things get complicated. It seems that [TSX](https://github.com/nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter-textobjects/blob/master/queries/tsx/textobjects.scm) and [JSX](https://github.com/nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter-textobjects/blob/master/queries/jsx/textobjects.scm) do not have already defined queries with tag captures there. Now, if you'd want to select attribute using tree-sitter parsing, it should have been `"parameter.outer"` and `"paramter.inner"`, as those are defined captures.

So, as far as I understand (I am no expert in both tree-sitter and TSX/JSX), there is currently no way to select tags with tree-sitter and 'nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter-textobjects' queries. You'd have to either find another appropriate queries out there or write your own (and PR to 'nvim-treesitter-textobjects' ;) ).

reply_data.body:
Neovim 0.10 has an updated default color scheme which might affect how your color scheme behaves.

By default highlight groups of 'mini.hipatterns' [link to similar built-in `Diagnostic*` groups](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/c43447661f4d3285352096cbb2c6e6ae7591bdd2/lua/mini/hipatterns.lua#L711-L714) which might have affected how they are displayed for you now.

The way to ensure that module's [highlight groups](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/c43447661f4d3285352096cbb2c6e6ae7591bdd2/doc/mini-hipatterns.txt#L85-L92) are the way you want them to, is to define them as any other highlight group. For example, with `:highlight` command (see `:h hi`) or `vim.api.nvim_set_hl()` Lua function (see `:h nvim_set_hl()`). Or use color scheme which explicitly defines those highlight groups (like 'mini.hues').

reply_data.body:
> Let's assume we have two sessions, each has its own working directory, different from each other.
> ...
> So my question would be is it possible to change cwd of the session when switching sessions? Thank you in advance.

I'd just like to be sure: what do you mean by "each has its own working directory"? Does it mean the actual "current working directory" of Neovim (a.k.a. `:h current-directory` which you can see with `:pwd`)? If it is, then it is usually restored when session is read.

'mini.sessions' directly relies on Neovim's built-in notion of sessions (which comes almost exactly from Vim). Configuration of what is saved in those can be done with 'sessionoptions' option. By default it already contains `curdir` value, which means that it saves Neovim's current directory to later restore. You can look at text inside session file (on Unix they are stored in '~/.local/share/nvim/session' directory) and verify that there is a `cd ...` call near the top (I have it on line 6).

------

However, my *suggested* solution (which I use from the very beginning and find super handy) is to set up auto changing of current directory based on the current buffer. This way you don't have to rely on sessions saving cwd and have it always up to date according to the file you edit.

There is a [`MiniMisc.setup_auto_root()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/335fdd637e905c5cdb8d7e7a9602e38cea9193af/doc/mini-misc.txt#L119) function just for that purpose. Its actual usage should be [quite straightforward](https://github.com/echasnovski/nvim/blob/0ed594cc06adfe40c6003ec7fd839d2e26ffa5c6/init.lua#L219-L220).

------

> Now I'm trying to migrate as many of my plugins to mini ones as possible. I really like them, thank you for your efforts and sharing.

Then I'd like to interest you in some ['mini.files'](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/readmes/mini-files.md) instead of 'oil.nvim' :)

reply_data.body:
> I opened a file like `nvim lua/plugins/sessions.lua`, and then do some editing, open another file like `files.lua` and close `sessions.lua` file, then exit nvim. Next time I re-opened nvim without parameters. There should be only `files.lua` itself, while `sessions.lua` is opened, too.

It depends on what you mean by "close `sessions.lua` file". If it is not made visible, then it is not closed per se, just hidden. Neovim does not really operate with files, but buffers (see `:h windows-intro`).

To properly "close" a buffer, either `:bwipeout` it or [`MiniBufremove.wipeout()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/335fdd637e905c5cdb8d7e7a9602e38cea9193af/doc/mini-bufremove.txt#L85) (that's what I do; `MiniBufremove.delete()` should also work).

> If that is not the expected routine to use sessions, could you share how you use it? Thank you in advance.

The way I use it is basically:
- To start a new session execute explicitly `MiniSessions.write('new-session')`. It will be autowritten before Neovim is correctly closed.
- To resume existing session, pick the one from 'mini.starter' (enough for at least 99% of startups) or via `MiniSessions.select()` when already editing some other buffers (or 'mini.starter' does not list target session as it was edited too long ago).

That's basically it. I don't use local sessions (and can't really recommend using them), only global. The explicit loading is a benefit for me, but it can certainly not be like that for others.

reply_data.body:
Hi!

'mini.tabline' doesn't have a lot of configurable features: it just shows all "good" (a.k.a. listed) buffers in the fixed order (based on buffer identifier). It does not allow custom ordering, specific mappings, or something else. It *does* support clicking with mouse to make the buffer current, though.

Removing buffers with 'mini.bufremove' (either `wipeout` or `delete`) can indeed make using 'mini.tabline' better, and that is what I am using.

Navigating to a specific buffer can be done either with [`buffer` target of 'mini.bracketed'](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/6260c7d3d96efdaaf5dece53457584ece5cf7212/doc/mini-bracketed.txt#L36) or [built-in `buffers` picker from 'mini.pick'](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/6260c7d3d96efdaaf5dece53457584ece5cf7212/doc/mini-pick.txt#L1119) (with `:Pick buffers` command typed manually or inside mapping). I use both depending on the buffer, session, and mood.

You can also take a look at using Neovim's built-in "alternate buffer" feature. I use it in the following mapping: `vim.keymap.set('n', '<Leader>ba', '<Cmd>b#<CR>')`.

But in fact when I search using lowercase the results are also lowercase. May I ask how to truly enbale ignoring case? Thank you.
```
- Both `stritems` and `query` depend on values of 'ignorecase' and 'smartcase'.
  If query shows "ignore case" properties (only 'ignorecase' is set or both
  'ignorecase' / 'smartcase' are set and query has only lowercase characters),
  then `stritems` and `query` will have only lowercase characters.
  This allows automatic support for case insensitive matching while being
  faster and having simpler match function implementation.
```

Yes, *default matching* ignores depending on the value of 'ignorecase'/'smartcase' options and the casing of the query. Exactly how is described in the quote you provided.

If you don't get expected matches with different casing with only lowercase query, make sure that:
- You have 'ignorecase' and/or 'smartcase' options set. See `:=vim.o.ignorecase` and `:=vim.o.smartcase`.
- You use default matching. It is used in all pickers by default except `grep_live` (and maybe `resume` if it resumes `grep_live`), which uses matching of underlying CLI tool. You'd have to [configure them separately](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/19e1584124cda35388d4fdb911eab7124014e541/doc/mini-pick.txt#L79-L84) if this is the case you're having trouble with.

reply_data.body:
> hi [echasnovski](https://github.com/echasnovski), for `mini.clue`, is it possible to let width and height be auto, at the same time to set clue window centered. Currently I can set fixed width and height, with the clue window centered. And also I could find `SW`, `NW`, `SE` and `NE` options without an option `center` or such like. Thank you for any help!

Yes, this is possible, but not entirely trivial. Mostly because I discourage using centered window for 'mini.clue', as it is too intrusive.

Overall window config can be configured using [`config.window.config`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/ebc8cb0c1f73ee6c53e0560957a37a2307a70f98/doc/mini-clue.txt#L557) config entry, which can also be a callable (function). Here is [an example of how to use it](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/ebc8cb0c1f73ee6c53e0560957a37a2307a70f98/doc/mini-clue.txt#L450-L467).

Height is already automatically computed based on content (number of clues). Width can also be automatically computed by using `width = 'auto'` instead of a number (it is a special case in how 'mini.clue' processes `window.config`).

Centering window should be done inside callable `window.config` by computing proper `row` and `col` of the window. Such that it takes half of available leftover height/width. Here is one example of how to do it (leveraging "dynamic width" approach from [here](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/issues/855#issuecomment-2094793829)):

```lua
local compute_dynamic_width = function(buf_id)
  local max_width = 0.4 * vim.o.columns
  local widths = vim.tbl_map(vim.fn.strdisplaywidth, vim.api.nvim_buf_get_lines(buf_id, 0, -1, false))
  table.sort(widths)
  for i = #widths, 1, -1 do
    if widths[i] <= max_width then return widths[i] end
  end

  return max_width
end

local round = function(x) return math.floor(x + 0.5) end

local win_config_center = function(buf_id)
  local height = vim.api.nvim_buf_line_count(buf_id)
  local width = compute_dynamic_width(buf_id)
  return {
    height = height,
    width = width,
    anchor = 'NW',
    row = round(0.5 * (vim.o.lines - height)),
    col = round(0.5 * (vim.o.columns - width)),
  }
end

require('mini.clue').setup({
  -- Other relevant setup
  window = { config = win_config_center },
})
```

reply_data.body:
This looks like an effect of 'winblend' option being more than 0 while 'termguicolors' is off. You can check it with `:echo &winblend` and `:echo &termguicolors` (shows 0 if disabled, 1 if enabled). This affects all floating windows, not only from 'mini.files'.

If 'termguicolors' is not enabled with Neovim 0.10, then likely your terminal emulator does not support it. Setting 'winblend' to 0 (`vim.o.winblend = 0`) should fix the issue.

> I now realize that the issue was really about `termguicolors`. it is disbaled somehow. do I have an approach to figure out which plugin does that?

Probably 'mini.basics' as well :)

As 0.10 has automated detection (after neovim/neovim#26407), 'mini.basics' (after resolving #632) does not enable 'termguicolors' by default on 0.10. This automated detection probably has difficulty working on windows when connecting to a remote Debian Linux.

If you mostly use modern terminal emulators, I'd suggest just adding `vim.o.termguicolors = true` to your config.

reply_data.body:
The error described the issue at hand. Moving to hunks requires them being computed, which in turn is only done in buffer with enabled 'mini.diff'. At every "good" buffer enter [there is an automated attempt to enable it](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/63c21a99e60ee59456faa4e5a245c59eeacac4d9/doc/mini-diff.txt#L121-L122) which also involves attaching the source. A buffer is "good" if it is valid, normal (i.e. not help, quickfix, scratch, etc.), listed, and for text (i.e. not image, pdf, etc.).

What types of buffer and source do you see this in? If it is the default source (i.e. [`git`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/63c21a99e60ee59456faa4e5a245c59eeacac4d9/doc/mini-diff.txt#L520)), then it usually means that the current buffer is not inside Git repository.

reply_data.body:
It is indeed intended to be done with `neigh_pattern`, which uses Lua patterns (see `:h lua-patterns`).

Something like this will setup 'mini.pairs' to add only single character if it is added directly after `\` or any alphanumeric character  (`%w`):

```lua
require('mini.pairs').setup({
  mappings = {
    ['('] = { neigh_pattern = '[^\\%w].' },
    ['['] = { neigh_pattern = '[^\\%w].' },
    ['{'] = { neigh_pattern = '[^\\%w].' },
    ['"'] = { neigh_pattern = '[^\\%w].' },
    ["'"] = { neigh_pattern = '[^\\%w].' },
    ['`'] = { neigh_pattern = '[^\\%w].' },
  }
})
```

@echasnovski Hey!
What if I nedd `mini.diff` just from time to time. Do we have any ability to toggle plugin?
comment_data.bodyHTML:
@echasnovski Hey!

comment_data.bodyText:
@echasnovski Hey!
What if I nedd mini.diff just from time to time. Do we have any ability to toggle plugin?

reply_data.body:
Hi!

You have several options (from least to most in scale):
- Use [`toggle()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/6260c7d3d96efdaaf5dece53457584ece5cf7212/doc/mini-diff.txt#L436) function to toggle 'mini.diff' in current buffer. Note that this will have effect until you exit and re-enter this buffer, as there is an automated enabling on every buffer enter.
- Use [buffer-local](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/6260c7d3d96efdaaf5dece53457584ece5cf7212/doc/mini-diff.txt#L73-L80) variable to toggle more permanently per buffer: `vim.g.minidiff_disable = not vim.g.minidiff_disable`. Beware that this will not have an immediate effect on already present visualization and might require an execution of `:edit` command to make it up to date. 
- Use similar global variable to toggle: `vim.g.minidiff_disable = not vim.g.minidiff_disable`. This will toggle 'mini.diff' globally for all buffers. Also might require `:edit` to make visualization up to date.

All these solutions are mostly designed to be used inside a user mapping of their choice.

reply_data.body:
> How to properly install `markdown-preview.nvim`? I did it this way buy preview doesn't work.

There are several issues here:
- Two nested `hooks` instead of one.
- `post_install` hook is executed right after plugin is installed but *before* its content is visible to current session. So delaying an execution of `mkdp#util#install` is the suggested solution here (I do it, anyways).

This is the full code I'd recommend using:

```lua
local add, now, later = MiniDeps.add, MiniDeps.now, MiniDeps.later

later(function()
	local build = function() vim.fn["mkdp#util#install"]() end
	add({
		source = "iamcco/markdown-preview.nvim",
		hooks = {
			post_install = function() later(build) end,
			post_checkout = build,
		},
	})
end)
```

> another plugin which doesn't work is `ts-comment`
> 
> ```
> 	add("folke/ts-comments.nvim")
> 	require("ts-comments").setup()
> ```

Adding these lines works for me. Here is the full config:

<details><summary>Full working config with 'folke/ts-comments'</summary>

```lua
-- Clone 'mini.nvim' manually in a way that it gets managed by 'mini.deps'
local path_package = vim.fn.stdpath("data") .. "/site/"
local mini_path = path_package .. "pack/deps/start/mini.nvim"
if not vim.loop.fs_stat(mini_path) then
	vim.cmd('echo "Installing `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
	local clone_cmd = { "git", "clone", "--filter=blob:none", "https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim", mini_path }
	vim.fn.system(clone_cmd)
	vim.cmd("packadd mini.nvim | helptags ALL")
	vim.cmd('echo "Installed `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
end

-- Set up 'mini.deps' (customize to your liking)
require("mini.deps").setup({ path = { package = path_package } })

-- Use 'mini.deps'. `now()` and `later()` are helpers for a safe two-stage
-- startup and are optional.
local add, now, later = MiniDeps.add, MiniDeps.now, MiniDeps.later

-- vim.cmd([[
--   call print()
-- ]])

later(function()
	local build = function()
		vim.fn["mkdp#util#install"]()
	end
	add({
		source = "iamcco/markdown-preview.nvim",
		hooks = {
			post_install = function()
				later(build)
			end,
			post_checkout = build,
		},
	})
end)

add("folke/ts-comments.nvim")
require("ts-comments").setup()
```

Two nested hooks instead of one.

	add({
		source = "iamcco/markdown-preview.nvim",

end)
```

reply_data.body:
> What is the basis of the recommendation of "as part of 'mini.nvim' library?

The main suggestion is to install 'mini.nvim' as a library and then call `setup()` only for modules that you want to use. Others will not be used, so no extra overhead. This will need one plugin installation entry in your plugin manager. Also you'll get access to information and updates from all modules (current and future new ones).

If you don't like extra help tags from plugins you're not using and/or want to go *extra* lightweight on disk usage, use standalone repositories. They will be updated *after* the change is merged into a main 'mini.nvim' plugin.

It does not work in Visual mode, only in Operator-pending mode (as in "after typing an operator", like `dgc` or `gcgc`).

There is no way to visually select comment block with built-in commenting (and defaults of 'mini.comment') by design: mostly because visual selection by itself is rarely an end goal, usually it is to perform some action on it. Hence "comment visual selection" is usually a more common action, it gets the preference for `gc` mapping in Visual mode.

With 'mini.comment' you *can* have ability to visually select comment block by [configuring different `mappings.textobject` and `mappings.comment_visual`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/a3f274633a57c713160baf51724ecfc051117877/doc/mini-comment.txt#L96-L101).

This can be done with the following patch (and perhaps there's an easier workaround):

```diff
From 57e6e2295c8fa3471f31712c897c2ca0849d7304 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: William Roy <wroy@proton.me>
Date: Fri, 9 Aug 2024 13:17:17 -0400
Subject: [PATCH] feat(tabline): hide unnamed buffer

---
 lua/mini/tabline.lua | 6 +++++-
 1 file changed, 5 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/lua/mini/tabline.lua b/lua/mini/tabline.lua
index d9c6228..2ea864b 100644
--- a/lua/mini/tabline.lua
+++ b/lua/mini/tabline.lua
@@ -262,7 +262,7 @@ end
 H.list_tabs = function()
   local tabs = {}
   for _, buf_id in ipairs(vim.api.nvim_list_bufs()) do
-    if H.is_buffer_in_minitabline(buf_id) then
+    if H.is_buffer_in_minitabline(buf_id) and not H.is_unnamed_buffer(buf_id) then
       local tab = { buf_id = buf_id }
       tab['hl'] = H.construct_highlight(buf_id)
       tab['tabfunc'] = H.construct_tabfunc(buf_id)
@@ -275,6 +275,10 @@ H.list_tabs = function()
   H.tabs = tabs
 end
 
+H.is_unnamed_buffer = function(buf_id)
+  return vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(buf_id) == ''
+end
+
 H.is_buffer_in_minitabline = function(buf_id) return vim.bo[buf_id].buflisted end
 
 -- Tab's highlight group
-- 
2.45.2
```

reply_data.body:
I don't think recommending patching plugins is a good idea. Making all unnamed buffers be unlisted is *relatively* straightforward:

```lua
local unlist_unnamed = function(data)
  local buf = data.buf
  if not (vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(buf) == '' and vim.bo[buf].buflisted) then return end
  vim.bo[buf].buflisted = false
end

local unlist_unnamed_all = function()
  for _, buf in ipairs(vim.api.nvim_list_bufs()) do
    unlist_unnamed({ buf = buf })
  end
end

vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd({ 'BufAdd', 'BufFilePost' }, { callback = unlist_unnamed })
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd({ 'VimEnter' }, { callback = unlist_unnamed_all })
```
