reply_data.body:
> I don't think recommending patching plugins is a good idea.

I personally believe that it’s fine. A plugin made configurable enough to satisfy everyone’s needs will never truly be possible—or, arguably, desirable. Patches give you the ability to separate from upstream for smaller changes without resorting to maintaining an actual fork. Moreover, modifying behavior using autocmd can also be seen as a form of hook (i.e. a way to extend or modify behavior dynamically), similar to applying a patch :p

reply_data.body:
> Patches give you the ability to separate from upstream for smaller changes without resorting to maintaining an actual fork.

The difference is that it needs an extra step during maintaining (if user wants it to persist across plugin updates). That is on top of an obvious issue that it modifies private code which can change (i.e. break patch for user) at any time.

Autocommands are completely independent of plugin and in this case provide a change more aligned with how 'mini.tabline' is designed to work.

reply_data.body:
The general idea is spot on. You stopped *just* before making it work. There are two approaches here:
- Disable *any* statusline in current window:
    ```lua
    vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', {
      pattern = { 'MiniStarterOpened' },
      desc = 'Disable statusline for starter',
      callback = function() vim.wo.statusline = '%#Normal#' end,
    })
    ```
    This showed to work in most common case of when Starter buffer is shown after startup. Needs more polishing to work after any `MiniStarter.open()`.
- Disable 'mini.statusline':
    ```lua
    vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', {
      pattern = { 'MiniStarterOpened' },
      desc = 'Disable statusline for starter',
      callback = function(data) vim.b[data.buf].ministatusline_disable = true end,
    })
    ```
    This works for all cases I've tested.

Make sure to not lazy load this autocommand creation.

Has anyone experimented with more complex sorting and filtering for mini.files? If so, do you have any tips for optimizing cache and performance?

I've recently been working with larger repositories and noticed that my custom sorting significantly impacts performance, especially when using the .gitignore someone shared here a while back. I quickly made a poor man's cache that works well enough to leave sorting files in a non-blocking background task, but I'm still hoping for a more practical solution:

---@module "mini.files"

---@type LazyPluginSpec
local Spec = {
  "mini.files", dev = true, dependencies = {{ "mini.icons", dev = true }},

  keys = {{
    "<leader>f",
    function()
      local file = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(0)
      local file_exists = vim.fn.filereadable(file) ~= 0

      MiniFiles.open(file_exists and file or nil)
      MiniFiles.reveal_cwd()
      MiniFiles.refresh({
        content = {
          sort = MiniFiles.sort,
          filter = MiniFiles.filter,
        },
      })
    end,
    desc = "Files"
  }},

  -- TODO:
  --
  -- Cache invalidation needs to be addressed, potentially right after
  -- synchronization. To achieve this we first need the machinery to notify
  -- when processing is complete (see the FIXME below).
  --
  opts = {
    content = {
      sort = function(fs_entries)
        local dirs = {}
        for _, fs in ipairs(fs_entries) do
          local dir = vim.fn.fnamemodify(fs.path, ":h")
          if not MiniFiles.gitignore_is_cached(dir) then
            if not vim.tbl_contains(dirs, dir) then
              table.insert(dirs, dir)
            end
          end
        end
        for _, dir in ipairs(dirs) do
          local id = vim.fn.jobstart({ "git", "check-ignore", "--stdin" }, {
            stdout_buffered = true,
            on_stdout = function(_, file)
              MiniFiles.gitignore_cache(dir, file)
            end,
          })
          local entries = {}
          for _, fs in ipairs(fs_entries) do
            if vim.fn.fnamemodify(fs.path, ":h") == dir then
              table.insert(entries, fs.path)
            end
          end
          -- This operation is non-blocking. Smaller repositories will
          -- filter out .gitignored files instantly, while large ones (e.g.,
          -- Chromium) will process in the background.
          --
          -- FIXME: There's nothing to notify when the processing is
          -- complete.
          --
          vim.fn.chansend(id, table.concat(entries, '\n'))
          vim.fn.chanclose(id, "stdin")
        end
        return MiniFiles.default_sort(vim.iter(fs_entries):filter(function(fs)
          local dir = vim.fn.fnamemodify(fs.path, ":h")
          return not MiniFiles.gitignore_is_ignored(dir, fs.path)
        end):totable())
      end,

      filter = function(fs_entry)
        return not vim.startswith(fs_entry.name, ".")
      end
    },

    windows = { max_number = 1 },
    options = { permanent_delete = false }
  },

  config = function(_, opts)
    require ("mini.files").setup(opts)

    MiniFiles.gitignore = {}
    MiniFiles.gitignore_cache = function(dir, files) MiniFiles.gitignore[dir] = MiniFiles.gitignore[dir] or {} for _, file in ipairs(files) do MiniFiles.gitignore[dir][file] = true end end
    MiniFiles.gitignore_is_cached = function(dir) return MiniFiles.gitignore[dir] ~= nil end
    MiniFiles.gitignore_is_ignored = function(dir, file)
      return MiniFiles.gitignore[dir] and MiniFiles.gitignore[dir][file] or false
    end

    local function toggle_state()
      MiniFiles.state = not MiniFiles.state
      MiniFiles.sort = MiniFiles.state and MiniFiles.default_sort or opts.content.sort
      MiniFiles.filter = MiniFiles.state and MiniFiles.default_filter or opts.content.filter
      MiniFiles.refresh {
        content = {
          sort = MiniFiles.sort,
          filter = MiniFiles.filter
        }
      }
    end

    vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("User", {
      pattern = "MiniFilesBufferCreate",
      callback = function(args)
        vim.keymap.set("n", ".", toggle_state, { buffer = args.data.buf_id })
      end
    })
  end
}

> I quickly made a poor man's cache that works well enough to leave sorting files in a non-blocking background task, but I'm still hoping for a more practical solution:

There are couple of things I'd approach differently:

- You can get all ignored paths in a single CLI command: `git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard`. This can be done once per repository per explorer session and cached the same way.
- All implemented tasks seem to fit in "filter" category. To optimize this, it might be reasonable to convert array of ignored paths to a map. For ignored files this is trivial, but ignored directories need recursive traversing all its entries which might be costly. If there are many ignored directories or a single *very* big directory, this will be less performant. Otherwise, doing only files in a map can save time. Checking ignored directories one by one if they are ancestor of a path in question should be not that slow.

Here's the solution I came up with:

```lua
config = function(_, opts)
  -- HACK:
  --
  -- Mini.Surround's `add` functionality operates with the 'a' text object by
  -- default, which includes surrounding whitespace when capturing. While
  -- this behavior may be acceptable in some contexts, for a surround plugin,
  -- we typically want text objects to focus solely on the text between
  -- delimiters.
  --
  -- Since Mini.Surround does not directly expose the necessary settings, we
  -- need to use introspection to access its internal H table, which is
  -- typically private, and then modify the `make_operator` function to use
  -- 'i' (inner) by default instead of 'a' (around).
  --
  local H = {}
  local function hook(_)
    local information = debug.getinfo(2, "nS")

    -- Inspect the call stack to find make_operator
    --
    if information and information.name == "make_operator" then
      local make_operator = debug.getinfo(2, "f").func
      local i = 1
      while true do
        local name, value = debug.getupvalue(make_operator, i)
        if name == "H" then
          H = value
          H.make_operator = function(task, direction, search_method, ask_for_textobject, textobject)
            return function()
              textobject = textobject or ''
              if H.is_disabled() then return [[\<Esc>]] end
              H.cache = { count = vim.v.count1, direction = direction, search_method = search_method }
              vim.o.operatorfunc = 'v:lua.MiniSurround.' .. task
              return '<Cmd>echon ""<CR>g@' .. (ask_for_textobject and textobject or ' ')
            end
          end
          H.apply_hook_logic = function()
            local config = H.get_config()
            local m = config.mappings
            local expr_map = function(lhs, rhs, desc)
              value.map("n", lhs, rhs, { expr = true, desc = desc })
            end
            expr_map(m.add, value.make_operator("add", nil, nil, true, 'i'), "Add surrounding")
            debug.sethook()
          end
          break
        end
        i = i + 1
      end
    end
  end

  debug.sethook(hook, "c")
  require("mini.surround").setup(opts)
  H.apply_hook_logic()
end
```

This is different than the iconic tpope surround.vim, where it's `s<motion><char>`. It took me a long time to get used to `sa` and takes an extra character to type. The tradeoff is that all of the surround mappings are under one key. Adding a surround `sa`, replacing one `sr`, deleting one `sd`.

After two years of trying out this way I'm still not convinced I love it but I wanted to at least give it a fair shot instead of being stubborn. In the end I think I'll probably stick with this syntax despite the most common usage having an extra key press than I am used to.

reply_data.body:
> As far as I can tell, the default keybinds `g[` and `g]` correspond to `navigate_to_next_start` and `navigate_to_next_end` in treesitter-textobjects, but is there a simple way to have keybindings for the backwards search functionality as well?

Not quite. They go to left and right side of the textobject that is found based on the `config.search_method`. So it is similar to moving to left or right edge of visual selection after `va<char>`, which with default `search_method` can be covering or next.

As for the question, there is a [`move_cursor()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e50cf9de614500a20e47cfc50e30a100042f91c3/doc/mini-ai.txt#L582). It is not used in more built-in mappings because combinations of "side" and "search method" start being confusing really quick.

You can use it, for example, like this:

```lua
local map_move_cursor = function(lhs, side, search_method)
  local rhs = function()
    local ok, tobj_id = pcall(vim.fn.getcharstr)
    if not ok or tobj_id == '\27' then return '' end
    local opts = { search_method = search_method, n_times = vim.v.count1 }
    MiniAi.move_cursor(side, 'a', vim.fn.escape(tobj_id, '\\'), opts)
  end

  local desc = string.format('Move to %s %s side', search_method, side)
  vim.keymap.set({ 'n', 'x', 'o' }, lhs, rhs, { desc = desc })
end

map_move_cursor('g{', 'left', 'prev')
map_move_cursor('g}', 'right', 'prev')
```

With this, `g{` / `g}` move to left/right side of the previous textobject.. This has at least 95% of functionality. The only thing lacking is seamless dot-repeat, as it would ask for textobject id each time. If this is too inconvenient, then going the built-in route of [returning `<Cmd>lua ... <CR>` string](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e50cf9de614500a20e47cfc50e30a100042f91c3/lua/mini/ai.lua#L1281-L1288) inside an [expression mapping](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e50cf9de614500a20e47cfc50e30a100042f91c3/lua/mini/ai.lua#L1168) is the only good solution here.

reply_data.body:
I am not sure how you have Copilot suggestions set up, so can't really explain why 'mini.completion' overrides it.

What I can say is that 'mini.completion' intentionally supports [only two sources](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e50cf9de614500a20e47cfc50e30a100042f91c3/doc/mini-completion.txt#L17-L30): LSP and fallback. So the best way to integrate Copilot with 'mini.completion' is one of the following:
- Make it part of LSP source. For example, attach a dummy LSP client that operates with Copilot.
- Make it part of fallback source. For example, check if there are copilot suggestions and fall back to built-in completion otherwise.

Unfortunately, I don't know a good/reasonable implementation to either of approaches.

reply_data.body:
The 'mini.completion' module supports only two "sources": LSP and fallback (used if there is no LSP candidates). By default fallback is equivalent to `<C-n>` built-in Insert mode completion, but it can be anything (including expanding snippets from 'friendly-snippets').

That said, I personally find snippets as completion items a bit distracting, so generally would not prioritize this workflow. Instead, the planned 'mini.snippets' (which I am developing and alpha-testing right now) has separate mechanism of matching and suggesting snippets (including the ones from 'friendly-snippets' if user chooses to use them in setup).

reply_data.body:
> What's the difference in how mini.hues initially handles chroma compared to how mini.colors handles it?

They use the same Oklch color space, so the computing chroma are the same.

They way 'mini.hues' deals with chroma is described [in algorithm overview](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e50cf9de614500a20e47cfc50e30a100042f91c3/doc/mini-hues.txt#L245). In particular, it treats foreground/background chroma and chroma value from `config.saturation` differently.

While `chan_set()` method of colorscheme from 'mini.colors' set channel to a certain value to [all highlight groups by default](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e50cf9de614500a20e47cfc50e30a100042f91c3/doc/mini-colors.txt#L552). For example, in this case it set chroma 5 to both background and foreground of `Normal` groups resulting in a saturated background.

> (which I have set to be very short)

This is the main problem here. Any mapping that consists from several characters *has* to be typed with at most 'timeoutlen' millisecond between each key press. This is how mappings in Neovim (and Vim) work.

If you rely on some other functionality that enhances mappings (like 'folke/which-key.nvim' or 'mini.clue'), then I'd suggest looking there. In 'mini.clue' it is as easy as adding `{ mode = 's', keys = 's' }` to [`config.triggers`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/848c5e8f428faf843051768e0d56104cd02aea1f/doc/mini-clue.txt#L494) and it works with very low 'timeoutlen'. I think setting 's' as trigger in 'which-key.nvim' should also solve the issue.

:wave:

> Do i need _mini.picker_ installed first then go to _mini.extra_ plugin as depencenices, or they independent?
> Because i see the readme of _mini.extras_ say they are extra pickers for.mini.pick

Yes, in order to use preconfigured pickers in 'mini.extra' there needs to be set up 'mini.pick'. So something like this:

```lua
require('mini.pick').setup()
require('mini.extra').setup()
```

With this added to the 'init.lua' you can now execute, for example, `:Pick explorer` (which is a user-friendly way for [`MiniExtra.pickers.explorer()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/61e5d46fc0cf71306c51275383767d996f559a60/doc/mini-extra.txt#L291)).

> Also, in _mini.git_, are there options like Gitsign for git folder as repo?

Sorry, I don't really understand the question.

'mini.git' is a Git CLI integration for Neovim. [Here are its features](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/61e5d46fc0cf71306c51275383767d996f559a60/doc/mini-git.txt#L8). Automated tracking should detect non-standard '.git' directory. Same goes for `:Git` user command if it is executed with current buffer inside detected Git repository.

That requires such support for CLI tool used for pattern search (which `rg` has) and passing those options/flags to it.
Both `grep_live` and `grep` have limited support of extra argument customization instead suggesting using [`builtin.cli()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/df1559e2ed7ece458e0a97a8bb9556d465d1c775/doc/mini-pick.txt#L1088-L1089) directly.

The answer is "yes", but it is not the best way to implement the "idea for context".

> My idea for context: grep live first opens a pick with all filetypes, the user can select one of those and then it opens a filtered grep live with that filetype, but if the query does not match any filetype then the user can write a valid regex e.g. `*foo.*.bar`

This is also possible with a new picker which implements the following approach:
1. Initial picker is opened via `MiniPick.start()` which has extensions/filetypes/something-else as items.
2. The picker also has custom `choose` action which takes the chosen item (extension/filetype/etc.) and opens another picker replacing present one.

Notes:
- The part of opening a first picker can be implemented as straightforward as `vim.ui.select()` call.
- I have [something similar in my config](https://github.com/echasnovski/nvim/blob/e6e3d5d66d62fcc6d93bcd227b1c85b1f2738a1a/init.lua#L313-L319): it lists entries in a specific directories and choosing one opens `files` picker with that directory as `cwd`.
- Instead of a separate picker as a first step, I'd recommend resorting to just using `vim.fn.input()` (or `vim.ui.input()` if you want something fancy) to get a filtering query from the user and then use it inside `MiniPick.builtin.cli()` call.

Finally i can made it work. Hey it look like a little complicated. But it work now . The code is not good enough. But at least it work 😂 😂 😂 
What is does : When you press `<Tab>` , it will create edit buffer without losing focus on `mini.pick`. 
If current the cursor is in directory and pressing `<Tab>` , it will **create** new `mini.pick` and cd it to that directory windows by calling `vim.cmd(":Pick explorer cwd='" .. selected_entry.path .. "'")`
Same behaviour with [[Neotree] Opening file without losing sidebar](https://github.com/nvim-neo-tree/neo-tree.nvim/wiki/Tips#open-file-without-losing-sidebar-focus)
### Code
```lua
 {
                "echasnovski/mini.pick",
                version = "*",
                opts = {
                    mappings = {
                        choose = "<CR>",
                        choose_in_vsplit = "<C-l>",
                        choose_in_split = "<C-j>",
                        toggle_preview = "",
                        execute = {
                            char = '<Tab>',
                            func = function()
                                local entries = require("mini.pick").get_picker_matches()
                                if entries and entries.all and entries.current_ind then
                                    local selected_entry = entries.all[entries.current_ind]
                                    if selected_entry.fs_type == "directory" then
                                        vim.cmd(":Pick explorer cwd='" .. selected_entry.path .. "'")
                                    else

                                        require("mini.pick").default_choose(selected_entry.path)
                                    end 
                                end  
                            end  
                        }
                        
                },
                }
            },

```

I am afraid this setup is a **very** bad idea. It will disable preview for *all* pickers, which I would not recommend.
Choosing any other key instead of `<Tab>` is a better idea. Otherwise having these mappings in a customized `explorer` picker (see [this example](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/df1559e2ed7ece458e0a97a8bb9556d465d1c775/doc/mini-pick.txt#L1204-L1209)) is also a good approach, since this code seems to be tailored for that picker specifically.

Also you can use `entries.current` directly. Here is how I'd rewrite the main function:

```lua
function()
  local current = (MiniPick.get_picker_matches() or {}).current
  if current == nil then return end
  if current.fs_type == 'directory' then return MiniExtra.pickers.explorer({ cwd = current.path }) end
  MiniPick.default_choose(current.path)
end
```

Although, this will both remove a picker name and leave empty spots without border, but that is the best it will get.

reply_data.bodyHTML:
Thanks for kind words!

'mini.pick' actions doesn't follow a regular mappings paths: it has its own key query process. This is needed to implement the "single window UI" design. For example, the query text you see at the top of the window is not an actual text and is specially updated after every key press from the user.

That said, having an extra key for choosing is not something 'mini.pick' was designed for. The "proper" approach is to make <Right> choose current match by setting config.mappings.choose to '<Right>', but I'd highly recommend against it: this will conflict with moving caret to the right and disable <CR>.

One hacky solution is to create custom action which would emulate pressing <CR> after user presses <Right>. This one seems to work:

require('mini.pick').setup({
  mappings = {
    caret_right = '',
    my_choose = { char = '<Right>', func = function() vim.api.nvim_input('\r') end },
  },
})

reply_data.body:
If this happens occasionally, I'd suggest creating a surrounding from [user prompt](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/7b4d5d48b6b5a75009d63f8f3e4ef4819b7e8139/doc/mini-surround.txt#L181). So that would be:
- Put cursor on `int` in Normal mode.
- Type `saiw?`.
- Type `Optional[` and `<CR>` for the left part.
- Type `]` and `<CR>` for the right part.

If you encounter this often (as I assume you do :) ), I'd suggest "investing" into creating custom surrounding. As it is a name in front of the brackets, the "array" name seems reasonable. So it can be something like:
```lua
local surr_arr_output = function()
  local arr_name = MiniSurround.user_input('Array name')
  return { left = arr_name .. '[', right = ']' }
end
require('mini.surround').setup({
  custom_surroundings = {
    a = { input = { '%f[%w_%.][%w_%.]+%b[]', '^.-%[().*()%]$' }, output = surr_arr_output },
  },
})
```
Now adding is a bit simpler (and requires no `[` and `]`):
- Put cursor on `int` in Normal mode.
- Type `saiwa`.
- Type `Optional` and `<CR>`.

This also has all the added benefits of a regular custom surrounding:
- `sda` now can delete (any) array-like surrounding. So it can convert `Optional[int]` back to `int`.
- `sraa` (followed by the replacement name) can replace it with another. So it can convert `Optional[int]` into `Array[int]`.
- And more: `sfa`, `sha`, etc.

------

> I'm thinking off something that would allow me to stay in insert mode and type:
> 
> `Optional|int` then press a mapping (say, `<C-s>`) and enter a motion for the surround.

My personal suggestion would be to get accustomed for exiting into Normal mode frequently for such text editing. Using `<C-o>` occasionally  is also ok, of course.

reply_data.bodyHTML:
Welcome!

  1. How do I show the relative path (or just the file name) in the statusline instead of the absolute path?

Where exactly do you want to show only file name? If as on screenshot, then it is configured in config.content.inactive. It can be set to the function which uses '%t' string to show file "tail" instead of currently used '%F' to show full path. So something like this would be enough:

require('mini.statusline').setup({
  content = {
    inactive = function() return '%#MiniStatuslineInactive#%t%=' end,
  },
})

If it is in the active window, then it is a bit more complicated and involves setting config.content.active to custom function. The default content is present in the help file and it shows full path for windows wider than 140 columns and only filename for narrower ones. Adjusting that involves copying that function to your config/'init.lua' and adjusting it to fit your need.

2. I'm using NeoTree as a file explorer. How can I disable the statusline when NeoTree is open and prevent it from showing anything in the statusline?

All 'mini.nvim' modules can be disabled per buffer by setting dedicated buffer-local variable. For 'mini.statusline' it is vim.b.ministatusline_disable. Your case fits the "Disable for a certain filetype" disabling recipe.

reply_data.body: If you want relative path and not file name, then use `'%f'` (which is what `section_filename()` uses for narrower widths). It is a "Path to the file in the buffer, as typed or relative to current directory." (see `:h 'statusline'`). On practice this indeed usually means path relative to Neovim's current working directory (see `:h current-directory` and `:h :pwd`), which can be absolute if file is not inside current working directory.

This is my current setup for `mini.sessions`. I didn't like that local sessions are saved in the project's directory, so I used project's name to saved session file in the global session directory. Among other configurations

```

-- Sessions are named based on the project name (last folder in the project path)


-- Get the last folder name from the current working directory path 
-- to use as the session name
local last_folder = function()
  -- Remove trailing slash if present
  local path = vim.fn.getcwd()
  path = path:gsub("[/\\]$", "")
  
  -- Handle both Windows and Unix-style paths
  local last_folder = path:match("[/\\]([^/\\]+)$") or path:match("^([^/\\]+)$")
  
  -- Debug info
  vim.notify("Extracting folder name from path: " .. path .. " -> " .. (last_folder or "default_session"))
  
  return last_folder or "default_session"
end

-- Setup session directory and file
local session_dir = vim.fn.stdpath('data') .. '\\session'
if not vim.loop.fs_stat(session_dir) then
  vim.loop.fs_mkdir(session_dir, 511) -- 511 = 0o777
  vim.notify("Created session directory: " .. session_dir)
end

local function get_session_file()
  local full_path = session_dir .. '\\'.. last_folder()
  return full_path
end
      

-- Initialize mini.sessions
require('mini.sessions').setup({
  -- Disable local session because we are using project-based sessions 
  -- and session names are based on the project name
  file = '',  
  
  hooks = {
    pre = {
      write = function()
        vim.notify("Pre-write hook called")
          
        -- Save all modified buffers
        vim.api.nvim_exec('silent! wall', false)

        -- Close certain windows/buffers before saving session
        for _, buf in ipairs(vim.api.nvim_list_bufs()) do
          local buftype = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_option(buf, 'buftype')
          local filetype = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_option(buf, 'filetype')
          
          -- List of filetypes/buftypes to close before saving session
          local excluded = {
            filetypes = { 'Neo-Tree', 'neo-tree', 'qf', 'help', 'gitcommit' },
            buftypes = { 'terminal', 'help' }
          }
              
          -- Close if buffer matches exclusion criteria
          if vim.tbl_contains(excluded.filetypes, filetype) or vim.tbl_contains(excluded.buftypes, buftype) then
            vim.api.nvim_buf_delete(buf, { force = true })
          end
        end
      end,
    },
  }
})

-- Add an additional command to manually create/write a session
vim.api.nvim_create_user_command('SaveSession', function()
  local session_file = get_session_file()
  vim.notify("Manually saving session to: " .. session_file)
  require('mini.sessions').write(last_folder())
end, {})

-- didn't see the need for an autocmd on VimEnter because we are using mini.starter plugin which 
-- already shows a list of previous sessions on startup

-- Auto-command to save session on exit 
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("ExitPre", {
  callback = function()
    vim.cmd('silent! SaveSession')
  end,
  group = vim.api.nvim_create_augroup('AutoSessions', { clear = true }),
  desc = "Automatically manage Neovim sessions"
})
```

reply_data.body:
No problem, this is not *entirely* off-topic :)

The main font is Input Mono (Compressed Light) and the font used for icons is a fallback NerdFontsSymbolsOnly from [Nerd Fonts](https://www.nerdfonts.com) ([as recommended](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/ccfc6300a5c17387f2899f979ecc04f942bee2a0/doc/mini-icons.txt#L61-L63)).

The terminal emulator used was Ghostty, which is currently in closed beta but [soon should be public](https://mitchellh.com/writing/ghostty-is-coming). But other "modern" terminal emulators should render similarly. Make sure that icons have the space to the right so that they can "overflow" (see [this](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/ccfc6300a5c17387f2899f979ecc04f942bee2a0/doc/mini-icons.txt#L51-L57)).

I was curious and made a comparison with terminal emulators I have lying around:

Ghostty (with NerdFontsSymbolsOnly as fallback):

![icons-demo_ghostty](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e39e5f27-2724-41f8-b3ea-906e3c20113a)

Kitty (with no explicit fallback, using the one which is built-in):

![icons-demo_kitty](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/09554428-17c3-4fa0-90dd-2f78199f7521)

WezTerm (with no explicit fallback, using the one which is built-in; **but** with enabled [`allow_square_glyphs_to_overflow_width`](https://wezfurlong.org/wezterm/config/lua/config/allow_square_glyphs_to_overflow_width.html?h=overflow)):

![icons-demo_wezterm](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/88d2d15d-fb47-49fe-b447-1243609e14f1)

So it seems to be a matter of making sure that there is a font that supports Nerd font icons *and* that terminal emulator is configured to overflow special glyphs.

reply_data.body:
The `vim.bo` is a specifically built-in Lua way to get and set buffer-local options in the current Neovim session's Lua.
The `nvim_get_option_value()` is an API method that Neovim provides for third party programs to interact with the Neovim session. It so happens to be also available from inside current Neovim session's Lua as a method of `vim.api`.

Using any of the two is fine, but `vim.bo` is specifically designed to be more concise and be used in Lua configs and plugins.

The `vim.fn` is slightly different: it is a bridge to call Vimscript functions from inside current session's Lua. This involves converting Lua objects into Vimscript objects, performing operation, and convert back. This is usually negligible but should be taken into account. Usually it is fine using it (I personally prefer `vim.fn.line('.')` instead of `vim.api.nvim_win_get_cursor(0)[1]`), but there are limitations (like sometimes using inside libuv callbacks as in timer, etc.). Also, sometimes there is simply no `vim.api.nvim_xxx()` method for some Vimscript function (for example, dealing with virtual columns, i.e. column outside of actually present text).

So as usual, this is a case by case decision.

comment_data.body: When using mini.icons and the hl-groups what is the correct way to preserve the background when for instance used in a statusline or tabline?
comment_data.bodyHTML: When using mini.icons and the hl-groups what is the correct way to preserve the background when for instance used in a statusline or tabline?
comment_data.bodyText: When using mini.icons and the hl-groups what is the correct way to preserve the background when for instance used in a statusline or tabline?

reply_data.body:
Default 'mini.icons' highlight only define foreground colors, so they already should preserve the background color. The issue here is that statusline, tabline, and winbar by default combine highlights with 'Normal' highlight groups. Which is why you probably see background same as in normal window. This issue is the main technical reason of why 'mini.statusline' and 'mini.tabline' don't show colored icons.

The solution here is to either define custom variations of highlight groups specifically  for statusline, tabline, and winbar which would have the appropriate background. Or use Neovim 0.11 (current Nightly) with neovim/neovim#29976 merged if all you need is to combine with dedicated `StatusLine`, `TabLine`, and `WinBar` highlight groups. Or don't use colored icons.

Nice solution!

Just FYI (as I'd say there is no single correct answer here), you can also get the color of highlight group attribute with the following more Neovim/API/Lua approach: `string.format('#%06x', vim.api.nvim_get_hl(0, { name = group })[attr])`. It *might* be slightly faster, but at the same time *might* be more error prone (if attribute doesn't exist). And it is unnecessarily more complex as `nvim_get_hl()` returns hex in the decimal form (presumably for performance reasons as it is how it is stored internally).

A more efficient method would be to not swap and use them as is. I remember myself readjusting which key I press after finalizing this feature in 'mini.surround' (mostly because I used open and close brackets interchangeably). It is usually less troubles than it might seem initially.

But with swapping, I am afraid, explicit swapping is the only way to go. I'd also suggest adjusting "input" parts too, as they are different (you can check with sh( and sh) inside something like ( aaa )). So it would be something like this:

require('mini.surround').setup({
  custom_surroundings = {
    ['('] = { input = { '%b()', '^.().*().$' },       output = { left = '(',  right = ')' } },
    [')'] = { input = { '%b()', '^.%s*().-()%s*.$' }, output = { left = '( ', right = ' )' } },
    --- ...
  },
})

> can this issue be solved via config? thanks.

Yes: setting [`config.search_method`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/c6eede272cfdb9b804e40dc43bb9bff53f38ed8a/doc/mini-ai.txt#L456) to be `'cover'` will always try to find only covering textobject (instead of default 'cover_or_next' which first searches inside current line and only then inside neighborhood line). reply_data.body:
> Just curious if I am developing bad habits or if this is a fairly common practice when it comes to neovim hacking and vim.schedule really is that magical?

Sometimes yes, sometimes no. `vim.schedule(f)` is basically "Execute `f` after all currently planned tasks are executed". This can be a good choice (for example, inside some autocommand callback to ensure that all other autocommands are executed before doing something) or a bad choice (for example, this will usually mean that callback will be executed after a redraw, which is a common cause of flickering if `f` has any visual side effects).

comment_data.body:
I dynamically switch git worktrees withing one neovim instance often (using a fork of [this](https://github.com/ThePrimeagen/git-worktree.nvim) plugin). I noticed I can easily copy files between different instances of `mini.files` that have different folders as their anchor, which is great :) 

What does not seem to be possible, though, is to jump between bookmarks across worktrees quickly, without closing the current `mini.files` instance and reopening another one that's rooted in the same worktree that the bookmark was created in. It seems like [marks are local to each root folder](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.files/blob/84efb81e5207ae8c41f54abdafb79c6212fc0971/lua/mini/files.lua#L1250), and capitalized marks are not treated specially (unlike in vim itself). What I'd like to be able to do is use `mA` in one `mini.files` instances, and then `'A` in an instance with a different anchor, and still jump to my original mark. This allows quicker file operations across folders.

Alternatively, what would be even quicker is having multiple `mini.files` instances in parallel, and having some sort of picker that allows switching between them (and perhaps showing off two side by side, that could be very useful for this type of operation). This is probably a more opinionated/complex change though.

reply_data.body:
> I noticed I can easily copy files between different instances of `mini.files` that have different folders as their anchor, which is great :)

This is not officially supported and I'd recommend to not do that. It works purely because of the implementation, but actual support (with documentation and testing) is not planned. Mostly because this doesn't feel like a good fit for the 'mini.files' file system manipulation design ("edit as regular buffers -> synchronize -> confirm").

> It seems like [marks are local to each root folder](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.files/blob/84efb81e5207ae8c41f54abdafb79c6212fc0971/lua/mini/files.lua#L1250), and capitalized marks are not treated specially (unlike in vim itself). What I'd like to be able to do is use `mA` in one `mini.files` instances, and then `'A` in an instance with a different anchor, and still jump to my original mark. This allows quicker file operations across folders.

~~Yes, all bookmarks are local to the current "explorer session". During initial testing I found that persistent bookmarks can become a problem when they accumulate (a bit confusing overall plus pollute the `g?` window). Here is [an example of a more persistent bookmarks](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2435d0de00174a45d6b352fefeaa6008ebe9f23b/doc/mini-files.txt#L531-L546).~~ This is mostly not true, as bookmarks indeed persist in history and are there with [`use_latest` equal to `true` in `MiniFiles.open()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2435d0de00174a45d6b352fefeaa6008ebe9f23b/doc/mini-files.txt#L725-L726). My mistake.

_**Edit**: this is not really needed, but can be an example of how to manipulate bookmarks_:
In the similar vain, you can make "in session" bookmarks persist per anchor with a bit of bookkeeping and proper autocommands:

```lua
local bookmarks_per_anchor = {}
local save_bookmarks = function()
  local state = MiniFiles.get_explorer_state()
  bookmarks_per_anchor[state.anchor] = state.bookmarks
end
local restore_bookmarks = function()
  local state = MiniFiles.get_explorer_state()
  for id, data in pairs(bookmarks_per_anchor[state.anchor] or {}) do
    MiniFiles.set_bookmark(id, data.path, { desc = data.desc })
  end
end
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', { pattern = 'MiniFilesExplorerClose', callback = save_bookmarks })
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('User', { pattern = 'MiniFilesExplorerOpen', callback = restore_bookmarks })
```

> Alternatively, what would be even quicker is having multiple `mini.files` instances in parallel, and having some sort of picker that allows switching between them (and perhaps showing off two side by side, that could be very useful for this type of operation). This is probably a more opinionated/complex change though.

This is already possible by opening explorers in different tabpages (`:h tabnew`). But again, I'd not recommend do file system manipulation across different explorer sessions.

> The anchor directory in which explorer is opened is there mostly to keep track of explorer state. You can go outside of it (with default h) if you have to. So to navigate to different worktree directory: press h until in worktree's parent, navigate to target worktree directory, press l.

I understand that this is possible, but it does not make it easy to quickly switch between different (working) directories attached to different buffers. I think my issue is that the anchor is actually important, since 1. it influences the bookmarks that are remembered, and 2. is the location we jump back to when resetting the tree, but that it is cumbersome to control.  Let met try to explain my use-case a bit better.

Say that I want to copy some files from a `path_a` to a `path_b` in my file system, then ideally I'd like to bookmark both paths in `mini.files` so I can jump back and forth between them quickly (I can also use one path as the anchor and bookmark the other). However, if I open `mini.files` under `path_a` (so it becomes the anchor), jump to `path_b`, notice that I need to make some edits to a file under `path_b`, close `mini.files`, and reopen it from some file under `path_b`, my bookmarks will not have been remembered, since I'm now using a new anchor directory (namely `path_b`). This use case occurs quite often in my workflow (either between different folders or different git worktrees), and is why I've been looking for a filetree plugin in neovim that (ideally) allows me to have multiple simultaneous instances between which I can copy/move files/folders, or at least allows me to efficiently transfer state within a single instance (using e.g. bookmarks).

As a workaround, I could find a common root for `path_a` and `path_b`, and always open `mini.files` with that common root as an anchor, so that my bookmarks are remembered and I don't have the clutter of persistent bookmarks. However, this common ancestor folder is often not the folder I want to jump to when I call `reset`, and I don't want to have to specify it manually. 

Additionally, what makes this more difficult to set up, is that there is no easy way to change the anchor or set it to a different folder than the folder of the file we are currently  `.open`ing. For example, the solutions [here](https://www.reddit.com/r/neovim/comments/1fzfiex/open_minifiles_on_current_directory_focused_on/) will have the anchor set to the folder of the current file, rather than the workspace root, which is (probably?) not what you want, since it makes it so every folder you open under the current project's `cwd` has its own bookmarks. A way to fix this would be to open `mini.files` in the root first, and only then jump to the open file or use `set_bookmark` to make a bookmark for it.

As you perhaps already suggested, `mini.files` might just not have been designed with such a use case in mind: I see it as a general file explorer with very nice & intuitive editing semantics, but that might not align with your plans for it. I think implementing persistent bookmarks is probably sufficient to implement the above use case (although it would be nicer if these bookmarks could be visually separated to avoid clutter), but having more control over the anchor seems like it would be useful as well.

However, if I open mini.files under path_a (so it becomes the anchor), jump to path_b, notice that I need to make some edits to a file under path_b, close mini.files, and reopen it from some file under path_b, my bookmarks will not have been remembered, since I'm now using a new anchor directory (namely path_b). This use case occurs quite often in my workflow (either between different folders or different git worktrees), and is why I've been looking for a filetree plugin in neovim that (ideally) allows me to have multiple simultaneous instances between which I can copy/move files/folders, or at least allows me to efficiently transfer state within a single instance (using e.g. bookmarks).
As a workaround, I could find a common root for path_a and path_b, and always open mini.files with that common root as an anchor, so that my bookmarks are remembered and I don't have the clutter of persistent bookmarks. However, this common ancestor folder is often not the folder I want to jump to when I call reset, and I don't want to have to specify it manually.
Additionally, what makes this more difficult to set up, is that there is no easy way to change the anchor or set it to a different folder than the folder of the file we are currently  .opening. For example, the solutions here will have the anchor set to the folder of the current file, rather than the workspace root, which is (probably?) not what you want, since it makes it so every folder you open under the current project's cwd has its own bookmarks. A way to fix this would be to open mini.files in the root first, and only then jump to the open file or use set_bookmark to make a bookmark for it.
As you perhaps already suggested, mini.files might just not have been designed with such a use case in mind: I see it as a general file explorer with very nice & intuitive editing semantics, but that might not align with your plans for it. I think implementing persistent bookmarks is probably sufficient to implement the above use case (although it would be nicer if these bookmarks could be visually separated to avoid clutter), but having more control over the anchor seems like it would be useful as well.

The "... notice that I need to make some edits to a file under `path_b`, close `mini.files`, and reopen it from some file under `path_b` ..." seems like the core issue here. The easy suggestion is to try and not do that: finish file manipulation, synchronize, and only then proceed with making edits.

------

Other suggestions are more in line of shaping your 'mini.files' workflow to better fit this case.

> A way to fix this would be to open mini.files in the root first, and only then jump to the open file or use set_bookmark to make a bookmark for it.

This would be one way of doing this. My first idea is to create a separate mapping that opens 'mini.files' explorer in the whole project root and not in worktree's root. Or automate it with fallback to current working directory, but I'd personally prefer explicit approach.

This is also a third approach, yes. You can indeed implement persistent bookmarks either across all anchors (easy) or within anchors which are part of a single big Git repo thus sharing them only across worktree directories (hard).

------

The 'mini.files' assumption is indeed that different anchors represent different projects (and current working directories). The ability to [open file in its directory](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2435d0de00174a45d6b352fefeaa6008ebe9f23b/doc/mini-files.txt#L709-L710) together with [reveal current working directory](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2435d0de00174a45d6b352fefeaa6008ebe9f23b/doc/mini-files.txt#L169) is more of an afterthought, but more or less a useful one.

All in all, I don't think adjusting 'mini.files' design/capabilities to fit the "allow editing file in the middle of file system manipulation" is a reasonable idea. It looks more like adjusting user workflow and/or config type of situation.

> I dont see the `cwd` as a separate abstraction necessarily; I'd just have an optional `anchor` argument to `MiniFiles.open`, which the user can pass whatever they want into, including the current value of the `cwd`. If the `file`'s path is not under this `anchor`, you indeed have to make an arbitrary choice on what to do, which -I assume- is why you don't like this.

There is no `file`, no `anchor`, no `cwd` arguments. There is a single [path](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2435d0de00174a45d6b352fefeaa6008ebe9f23b/doc/mini-files.txt#L720-L724) which is designed for directory path. This path will be used as id when storing history and the one shown after `reset()`. As "show current file in its parent directory" is a common use case, `path` argument was extended to allow file path. As both storing history and `reset()` require directory path, the "anchor" abstraction was introduced: same as `path` for directory path and file's parent for file path.

Any other changes to what branch is shown after `open()` are expected to be tweaked by the user with provided [helpers](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2435d0de00174a45d6b352fefeaa6008ebe9f23b/doc/mini-files.txt#L770-L920) and [events](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/2435d0de00174a45d6b352fefeaa6008ebe9f23b/doc/mini-files.txt#L328-L353). No new changes to the design are planned.

Currently it is a `detail` value of each [`CompletionItem`](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.18/specification/#completionItem) which is meant as "A human-readable string with additional information about this item, like type or symbol information.". LSP server is allowed to not pass it, and this is apparently what happens with Typescript. This will be addressed in #1258.

reply_data.body:
Hi! Likewise!

> I can't manage to have https://github.com/kristijanhusak/vim-dadbod-completion working with mini.completion, is it possible to configure them together?

The 'mini.completion' [supports only two "sources"](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/e91e854299429c986888711668743711acd8a14b/doc/mini-completion.txt#L17-L30) (which are applied consecutively): LSP and fallback. So there can be only two ways of achieving that:
- Turn 'vim-dadbod-completion' into a separate LSP server.
- Use the built-in omnifunc as a fallback. The first approximation of this might be something like this:
    ```lua
    autocmd FileType sql lua vim.bo.omnifunc = 'vim_dadbod_completion#omni'; vim.b.minicompletion_config = { fallback_action = '<C-x><C-o>' }
    ```

reply_data.body:
Thank you! I made it work. Omnifunc was overwritten each time an SQL buffer was saved with my mini.completion configuration :

```lua
        lsp_completion = {
          source_func = "omnifunc", -- <- set it to completefunc
          auto_setup = true,
        },
```

ended up with this autocmd in my plugin init function : 
```lua
      vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd({ "FileType" }, {
        pattern = { "sql", "mysql", "plsql" },
        callback = function()
          vim.bo.omnifunc = "vim_dadbod_completion#omni"
          vim.b.minicompletion_config = { fallback_action = "<C-x><C-o>" }
        end
```

With surprisingly heavy heart I am going to close this discussion. Exactly three years after it was created. Now the only preferred way to ask a question about configuration and usage of 'mini.nvim' is to [create a separate "Q&A" discussion](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/discussions/new?category=q-a).

Thank you all for three years of curiosity about 'mini.nvim'!
